The Master attained realization through his study of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. He went to Caoxi, where the Sixth Patriarch granted him certification.
Upon the Master’s arrival, he encountered the Patriarch seated; he circumambulated the meditation platform three times and struck his staff once.
He stood there with an air of self-importance. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand codes of dignified conduct and the eighty thousand subtle practices;
every action must be without flaw. Great Virtue, from what direction have you come to give rise to such great arrogance?

The Master replied, "The matter of birth and death is great, and impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-arising and understand that there is no swiftness? The Master replied:
“The essence is itself non-arising; it is understood that from the beginning there is no swiftness. The Patriarch said, “So it is, so it is. After a short while, the Master took his leave with a bow.
The Patriarch asked, “Is your return not too swift? The Master replied, “Since the essence is fundamentally neither moving nor still, how could there be swiftness?

The Patriarch asked, “Who knows that it is not moving? The Master replied, “It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to such discrimination. The Patriarch said, “You have truly attained the state of non-arising.”

The Master said, "In non-arising, how could there be intention? The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who is it that gives rise to discrimination? The Master said, "Discrimination, too, is not intention.
The Patriarch sighed in praise, saying, "Excellent! Excellent! Having received this seal of approval, one may then be called a realized one.

This Great Samādhi is fully endowed with manifold dharmas: first, the primary orthodoxy is not a divergent realization; second, perfect resonance is not a void realization;

It is said: "To study the Way, one must first have an awakening; it is like once having raced a swift dragon boat.
Though it be an old hall and empty ground, only after winning it once does one finally rest. Inferring from this, one must achieve a brilliant breakthrough and realization before it can be attained.
Therefore it is said: "The first phrase is known only by those of the same path."
"One who has severed study and is non-active is a person at leisure.
To have severed study means to sever worldly study and to study the study of non-action (*wuwei*). This is because worldly study does not lead to transcendence.
To study non-action means not to abide in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) of the Lesser Vehicle, but to enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the Mahāyāna.
The conditioned phenomena of the Hīnayāna are not ultimate. A Bodhisattva who studies Prajñā merges with the Dharma;

regarding all dharmas, they should have no place of abiding. Their mind is without obstruction, attaining great mastery. They act without acting and perform without performing; thus it is said they are "beyond study and non-active.
One who is a "leisurely practitioner of the Way" is one who accords with the Way and does not...
Because one is bound and fettered by worldly defilements (*kleśa*), it is called "leisure" [in the sense of being at ease with them].

This is truly because all sentient beings, from beginningless time until this very day, have turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*). Amidst every thought-moment regarding all external realms, they pursue these objects without ever relinquishing them for even a moment;
how, then, could they achieve liberation? A practitioner of the Way is able to transform the myriad things and is not [bound] by them.
While the myriad things revolve before one’s eyes in a thousand variations, the mind remains tranquil in a single realm. By the waterside and beneath the forest trees, one nurtures the sacred embryo;
gazing at the moonlight with carefree ease, listening to the sound of the spring with sovereign freedom. Thus it is said:
"The man of the Way is one who has transcended learning and is non-active."
"Do not eliminate deluded thoughts, nor seek the Truth.

What is called "deluded thought" refers to false and illusory conceptualization. This is truly because, throughout the twelve periods of the day, the攀緣 (pān-yuán) mind of all sentient beings is without interruption.
The mind is like a turtle longing for water; the will is like one [reaching out] to meet...
The horse of wind never ceases; therefore, it is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). That which is called "True" is precisely the one true Buddha-nature.
Now, this practitioner of the Way accords with the Dharma and does not fall into either of the two paths of the ordinary or the sage; he likewise distinguishes himself from those of the Two Vehicles.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle loathe and seek escape from the birth-and-death of the world, desiring to seek that which lies outside the realms.
Nien-pan: A Bodhisattva who studies Prajñā realizes that the myriad dharmas all return to oneself;
therefore, it is said, "Do not eliminate delusive thoughts, nor seek the Truth. Thus, Master Xiu said: "The dharmas of ordinary beings are fully present, yet ordinary beings do not know them."
To be fully endowed with the dharmas of a sage is for the sage not to meet [them]. If a sage were to meet them, he would be an ordinary person;
if an ordinary person were to know them, he would be a sage. These two statements share one principle but have two meanings. The Tradition says:
"If you can discern this, there will be no hindrance to finding a point of entry into the Buddha-dharma. If you cannot discern it, do not say that you have no doubts."
The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature.
Ignorance refers to the absence of the illumination of great wisdom (*prajñā*). Buddha-nature refers to the ultimately pure awakened nature.
That one has lived in vain and died in delusion from time immemorial, unable to achieve liberation, is entirely due to this ignorance.
It flows and revolves within clarity. Thus, we know that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the very root of affliction.

It serves as the fruit of the eighty-four thousand defilements and acts as the head of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). The afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges arise from this;

the cycle of saṃsāra through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust does not cease because of it. Even after emerging from the meditative state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), one returns to the body of a wildcat. This is ignorance.
Remaining within the pit is still the practice of illness. An ancient master said: "It is as swift as a flash of lightning and as violent as a raging wind;
the arising of worldly toil is swifter than a torrential stream, and the formation of the five desires is more urgent than a spinning wheel.
Thus, the construction of the four Māras and the galloping of the ten afflictions are all caused by ignorance. This is because [the truth] has not yet been realized.
Ordinary people are deluded and take [ignorance] to be a real entity. Now, this practitioner of the Way uses the wisdom of prajñā to illuminate and penetrate ignorance;
thus, they clearly perceive the Buddha-nature. Therefore it is said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature."
The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Since one has realized that ignorance is itself Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), one should know that the illusory body is itself the Dharma-body.

Regarding what is called the Dharma-body, the teachings speak of the fivefold Dharma-body: first, precepts; second, concentration; third, wisdom; fourth, liberation; and fifth, the knowledge and vision of liberation.
This is wisdom and vision. The *Zhuan* says: "Wisdom is darkly merged with the true realm and exhausts all phenomena to take them as its body; thus it is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
'Dharma' takes the meaning of providing a track and sustaining; 'body' takes the meaning of accumulation.

This Dharma-body is able to provide a track for the arising of all phenomena and is able to universally encompass all phenomena. One who penetrates the Dharma realizes that [the self] is born from the conditions of parents."
The illusory body is itself the adamantine, eternally abiding, indestructible body. Therefore it is said: "The illusory, transformed, empty body is the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is fully awakened to the fact that there is not a single thing; it is the original source-nature, the true and heavenly Buddha.

By means of the wisdom of *prajñā*, one illuminates that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty. There is not a single thing; there are no boundaries or manifestations; there are no names.

It is only through forced designation that it is called the "Dharmakāya. Formerly, when the Venerable Fu of Taiyuan was serving as a presiding lecturer (*śāstrādhyāpaka*), he was expounding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
When he reached the section on the meaning of the Dharmakāya, a mendicant (*pravrajita*) who had been listening from below the seat asked the presiding lecturer:
The Master said, "What you just lectured upon was the Dharma-body of all Buddhas; which one, then, is the Dharma-body of you, the Preceptor?
The Preceptor replied, "How could there be two Dharma-bodies? The Master said, "It is like a person speaking of food—it will never satisfy hunger.

He continued, "If you wish to realize the source of the mind, take awakening as your standard. The Master said, "This is the extent of my explanation regarding the meaning of the Dharma-body. He then turned away.

He requested that the Master explain this to him. The Master said, "Cease your lectures for three or five days; sit in meditation in an empty room and realize the Dharma-body through direct experience.
The Master followed these instructions exactly, withdrawing from all external conditions and sitting upright in a quiet chamber.

A lifetime passes in vain; therefore it is said that the Dharmakāya, through its awakened realization, possesses not a single thing. As for the statement that "the fundamental source and original nature is the true, heavenly Buddha":
if one now returns to the root and reverts to the source without relying on cultivation or realization, only then will one know that one has been a Buddha from the very beginning.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, wherever the eye meets an object or encounters conditions, every single thing reveals the teaching and every phenomenon manifests the Dharma;

there is nothing that is not a Buddha-work. Thus, Faldeng said: "Who would believe that the True Celestial Buddha manifests compassion in tens of thousands of ways? The *liǎo* flowers bloom on the ancient bank;
the white egrets stand upon the sandy shore. Dewdrops fall as the court sedge grows long; the clouds gather and the mountain stream moon turns cold. Head after head, it reveals the teaching.
This is the instruction. Observe it closely and thoroughly:
the five aggregates are like floating clouds, coming and going in emptiness; the three poisons are like bubbles on water, vainly appearing and vanishing.
A student of the Dharma realizes that the five aggregates are unreal, just like floating clouds, and knows that the three poisons are illusory. Return [to this truth].

They are like bubbles on water. What are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are: first, form (*rūpa*); second, sensation (*vedanā*); third, perception (*saṃjñā*); fourth, mental formations (*saṃskāra*);

and fifth, consciousness (*vijñāna*). Form takes obstruction as its defining characteristic; sensation takes receiving and experiencing as its defining characteristic; perception takes conceptualization as its defining characteristic;

mental formations take flux and movement as their defining characteristic; and consciousness takes discernment as its defining characteristic. To fully understand these five aggregates is to realize the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). What...
Regarding the "three poisons," they are: first, greed; second, anger; and third, delusion. Greed arises toward favorable conditions; anger arises toward adverse conditions;
and to accept things through a lack of wisdom is delusion. To realize this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
Since the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are like clouds in the vast void, empty and coming and going of their own accord, the three poisons likewise [return to emptiness].

Among all the hells, these are the most severe and painful; therein, the suffering of one's transgressions is continuous without interruption. Now, regarding the Dharma...

Therefore it is said: "In a single kṣaṇa, the karma of Avīci Hell is extinguished."

These are the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Individually, they are called the ten thousand practices (*sahasra-caryā*). All these gates of practice are contained within a single thought-moment;

they are primordially perfect and complete. As for what are called the "six perfections," they are: giving (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Why are they all termed "perfections"? It is because each has its own specific antidote (*pratipakṣa), and thus they are called "crossings" (*pāra*).
Generosity transcends stinginess and greed; ethical discipline transcends transgressions; patience transcends anger; diligence transcends indolence;
meditative concentration transcends dullness and agitation; and wisdom transcends ignorance. Therefore, they are called the Six Perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

Regarding this gateway of the perfections, it is not that those of the Lesser Vehicle now practice the six perfections partially; rather, it is the Bodhisattvas at the stage of provisional capacity who concurrently cultivate the six perfections. Thus...

In the dream, the six realms of existence are clearly manifest; upon awakening, all is empty, and there is not even a great chiliocosm.

upon waking, all is void, and there is no great chiliocosm. As for what are called the "six destinies," they are:
first, humans; second, devas; third, asuras; fourth, hungry ghosts; fifth, animals; and sixth, hell-beings. Why is it that they are all termed "destinies" (*gati*)? It is because...

All sentient beings, in a single thought-moment, fall into delusion and confusion; their karmic consciousness becomes vast and aimless, and according to the power of their karma, they spontaneously enter the six realms of existence.

one pursues only the dust of the world, unaware of returning to the source. What is called "emptiness within emptiness" refers to the fact that all...

now, being in accord with Prajñā, it not only renders the sentient beings of the six realms empty, but even the manifested realm of the great trichiliocosm lacks substantial reality.
Therefore, it is said that after awakening, all is empty and there is no "great."
A thousand times over:
there is neither sin nor merit, neither loss nor gain. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire.

Having realized that the nature of all phenomena is empty, within this state of quiescent extinction there are no marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
Being in accord with the markless Dharma-gate of Prajñā, one does not rely on linguistic expression, discrimination, or debate. Therefore it is said:
There is neither sin nor merit; there is neither loss nor gain. Within the nature of quiescence, do not seek or inquire.
Until now, the mirror of dust has never been polished; today, it must be clearly broken open.
A single spark of spiritual brilliance is fundamentally non-dual and indistinguishable from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
It is simply because all sentient beings, since immeasurable kalpas past, have never encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to illuminate and reveal their true nature.
This is like a mirror covered in dust and soil, long obscured and darkened, unable to reflect objects; today, having finally met a spiritual friend...
Having clarified one’s own vision, sweep away the dust and grime. The original radiance suddenly breaks through, illuminating heaven and earth. Thus, the former masters said:
"The light of the mind surges forth, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects; its essence reveals the true and eternal, unconstrained by words and letters.
The nature of the mind is unstained and is fundamentally perfected of itself; simply by leaving behind delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness."
"Who is without thought? Who is without birth?
If, in truth, there is neither birth nor non-birth, then the former phrase negates emotion while the latter reveals the Dharma. As for "Who is without thought? Who is without birth?", it asks:
who is this person without thought, and who is this person without birth? The mental thoughts of a person arise and perish without interruption; as for that arising...
The extinction of the mind is as incalculable as a cluster of akṣa fruits; from moment to moment, there is no cessation.

Like the flickering of a lamp’s flame or the trickling of a stream of water, when walking the mind reaches throughout the ten directions, and when sitting the consciousness clings to the three periods of time.

Therefore it is said: "Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If there is truly neither birth nor non-birth—if one truly understands the principle of non-birth—one will not be stained by the appearance of birth in any phenomena (*dharma*), yet this does not obstruct the arising of the myriad dharmas.
Master Xiu said: "The myriad dharmas have no mark of birth; year after year comes spring. Thus it is said.
If, in reality, there is neither birth nor non-birth, then call for the mechanical wooden man and ask him:
"Seeking the Buddha through the application of effort, when will it be accomplished?
This is repeated as a further analogy to make it easy to understand. Thus far, because of this discourse, we have seen that after awakening, all is empty and there is no "Great" [Buddha-nature].
"Thousand. There is neither sin nor merit, neither loss nor gain. Within the nature of quiescence, do not seek or inquire.

Yongjia [Zhixian] was deeply concerned that later generations might follow the literal words and give rise to interpretations, thereby forming the view of nihilism; thus he specifically made these emendations.
A bodhisattva studying Prajñāpāramitā must encounter a spiritual friend to illuminate their own insight, so as to realize non-thought within the midst of thought. Within...

Within arising and ceasing, one awakens to non-arising and non-ceasing. If one were to claim that the perpetual absence of thought and non-arising constitutes the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), it would be like a wooden puppet operated by a mechanism;
though it lacks mental activity, there is no way for it to expect to achieve Buddhahood. Therefore, it is said: "When will it be accomplished?
"When" (*zǎo wǎn*) is a dialectical expression from Jiang and Zhejiang, meaning "at what time. It is equivalent to asking "when can it be?"
It is accomplished.
Let go of the four great elements; do not grasp at them. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along with eating and drinking.
The "four great elements" refer to earth, water, fire, and wind. Since beginningless time, in taking up and casting off bodies, one has always been [bound by them].
Bound by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), one lacks sovereignty. Now, having realized that the nature of the four great elements is empty, one attains mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*).
In water, one is entirely water; in fire, entirely fire; in earth, entirely earth. Thus, Master Xiushan said: "The earth element does not contain water, fire, or wind.
Since it is so for one element, it is the same for the four. The four great elements have never failed to be all-pervasive. They are pervasive.
How could there ever have been any intermingling throughout? It is like a thousand lamps in a single room, or like ten thousand images within a single mirror.

The four great elements have different names but no four distinct natures; the realms, bases, faculties, objects, and consciousnesses do not interpenetrate. If one understands this principle, [one realizes the truth].

Therefore, it is said that one "releases the four great elements. As for the instruction not to "grasp," since one has realized that the nature of the four great elements is empty, where else could one grasp?
Hence, it is said not to grasp. Within the state of quiescent extinction, one follows along with eating and drinking.

If one realizes that the four great elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist, then it is best to float or sink according to one's own will and to drink and feed according to conditions.
Thus, Beidu said: "Whether coarse, eat; whether fine, eat. Do not look at them from the perspective of an ordinary person's appearance.
There is neither coarse nor fine; above, in the Fragrant Accumulation [Heaven], there are no roots or stems. Therefore, it is said: "Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along..."
It is like drinking and pecking.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and entirely empty; this is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vajra-bodhi*).
It is not only that the characteristics of the four great elements are fundamentally empty, but all conditioned phenomena produced are likewise entirely empty and quiescent.
It is said that "all practices" does not refer to merely one practice, but extends to all manner of myriad practices; all of these are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the very beginning.
Thus, a sutra says: "This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements. That is to say:

hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and the impurities of the various parts all return to earth. Saliva, nasal mucus, pus, blood, lymph, spittle, and froth [return to water]."
Phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the large and small excretions all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement returns to wind.
When the four great elements separate from one another, where then does this illusory body abide? Therefore it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and entirely empty.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. Having realized that all dharmas are originally empty, [one attains liberation].

"Quiescence" (*jì*) refers precisely to being in resonance with the nature of Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vimala-bodhi*). However, all sentient beings employ it in their daily lives without realizing it;
thus, Prime Minister Pei said: "Those who are in perfect enlightenment all day long yet have never experienced perfect enlightenment are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)."

Those who seek to realize perfect enlightenment but have not yet reached its ultimate perfection are Bodhisattvas. Those who are fully endowed with perfect enlightenment and abide in the maintenance of it are Tathāgatas.
Therefore, it is said that this is precisely the Great Perfect Enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
It is called "definitive teaching" because it manifests the true Sangha. There are those who, unwilling to follow their own inclinations, investigate [this state]:
one who internally harbors the embryo of the sage speaks with extraordinary distinction, possessing words of boldness and freedom from hesitation; hence it is called "definitive teaching.
One who studies Prajñā realizes the mind and penetrates the source, completely forgetting all myriad concerns, majestic and dignified.
Walking alone through the three realms, he is the leader of the Dharma-gates and the guide for humans and devas; thus, he is called a "manifest true monk.

If there are those who are unwilling to accept this according to their own feelings—should anyone be unwilling to accept the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma I possess and attempt to challenge me with various worldly wisdoms—I simply allow them to do so.
This is a challenge posed by another. An ancient master said:
"Even if you were to fill the entire world-system of the ten directions with nothing but heads of inquiry to question me, it would not require more than this old monk’s single snap of his fingers.
It would respond universally to all levels, high and low, without the slightest discrepancy between before and after; yet I fear you may not have the faith to believe it."
"Directly cutting through to the source is what the Buddhas have certified; picking leaves and seeking branches is not for me.
To enter directly and instantaneously into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, without following the gradual stages of the teachings or traversing them step by step—this is why it is called 'direct.
As the former masters said: 'This very matter, if it were found within words and phrases, would be among the three vehicles and twelve divisions [of the scriptures].'"
Is it not the case that the Teachings are beyond verbal expression? For what reason, then, do you say there is a "separate transmission outside the teachings"?
This single Dharma alone clarifies the mind directly; one seeks only its root and does not pursue its branches. Therefore, it is said: "Directly cutting through to the source."
That which is sealed by the Buddha refers to the mutual confirmation and authorization of all Buddhas’ Dharma-gates by means of a single seal. This seal establishes them definitively;
their arising and completion are simultaneous, with no sequence of before or after. Therefore, it is called a "seal" (*mudrā*).

As for the phrase "I am not one who can pluck leaves and seek branches," this refers to the study of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), which is like plucking leaves from a tree: the number of such Dharma-gates is inexhaustible, leading only to needless exhaustion.
In the end, it provides no benefit; therefore, it is said, "I am not capable.
The *maṇi* jewel is unrecognized by people, yet it is personally held within the *tathāgatagarbha*. In Sanskrit it is called *maṇi*;
here it is translated as "wish-fulfilling jewel" (*cintāmaṇi*). Its essential nature is light and supple, and it is pure and in accordance with the Dharma. It is endowed with...
Among all merits, only this one jewel can serve as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature. Everyone possesses this jewel, yet why is it that they cannot enjoy its benefits?
It is because it is shrouded by the dust and grime of ignorance and thus cannot manifest of itself; therefore, it is said that "people do not recognize it.
As for the phrase "personally obtained within the Tathāgatagarbha," this maṇi-jewel is not something found in the mundane world.
Thus, one personally obtains this treasure within the Tathāgata’s secret treasury.

As for what is called the "Tathāgata-garbha," there is the Tathāgata-garbha that remains within the bonds of affliction, and there is the Tathāgata-garbha that has emerged from those bonds. Sentient beings are constantly shrouded by the three poisons and the afflictions of the five aggregates;
although they possess this precious treasury, they are unable to enjoy its benefits. This is termed the "Tathāgata-garbha remaining within the bonds."

Furthermore, if the three virtues of all Buddhas are brilliant, pure, and perfectly complete, encompassing all manner of merits within the Dharma-realm—this is called the Tathāgatagarbha free from entanglements.
Setting aside the "garbha" for a moment, which one is the pearl?
"Do you not see when a monk asked Nanquan: 'The mani-jewel no one recognizes; it is personally held within the Tathāgatagarbha. What is this 'garbha'?
The Master said, "That which comes and goes with you, Old Teacher Wang, is the garbha. The monk asked, "What is the jewel? The Master then called to the monk, "Master!

Grandmaster! The monk responded, "Yes? The Master said: *Note: This passage is a classic example from the *Wumen Guan* (Case 1) illustrating the non-duality of the absolute and the relative, where the Master points directly to the student's own functioning as the "Tathāgatagarbha" and his own responsive presence as the "mani-jewel."*
Go! You do not understand my meaning as you go. Do not say that this monk failed to recommend [the Way];
even if he were able to recommend it, I know that you have not yet grasped it through your groping.
The six kinds of spiritual functions are both empty and not empty; the single orb of radiant light is both form and not form.
This maṇi jewel has six apertures, which metaphorically represent the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*). When deluded, they become the six thieves who plunder one's own family treasure;
all the immeasurable merit and dharma-wealth are entirely stolen by these six thieves. If, however, one awakens...
This is called the sixfold divine function. When it is in the eye, it is called seeing; when in the ear, it is called hearing; when in the mouth, it is called speaking;
when in the feet, it is called running. Its functioning is inexhaustible. As for "empty yet not empty," this wondrous function cannot be seen as either existent or non-existent.
Therefore it is said: if one says it exists, it has no appearance and no form; if one says it does not exist—
The Sage takes this as spiritual; thus it is said that emptiness is not empty. As for "a single sphere of light, its color is not color":
this precious jewel has, from time without beginning, been brilliantly radiant and luminous, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
Therefore, one knows that true color is formless yet pervades the great chiliocosm. An ancient worthy said: "The verdant bamboo stalks are all the Truth."
Thus, every lush yellow flower is nothing other than Prajñā; hence it is said: "A single orb of light, neither form nor non-form.
Purifying the five eyes and attaining the five powers—only through direct realization can one know that this is difficult to fathom.

While all the sūtras speak of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the five powers (*pañcabala*), the present mention of the "five eyes" (*pañcacakṣus*) and the five powers is found, according to our examination of various sūtras and śāstras, only in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
Let us explain this according to the text. What are called the five eyes are: first, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*);

second, the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); third, the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*); fourth, the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*); and fifth, the buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). To be fully endowed with these five eyes constitutes...
The Tathāgata immediately attains the manifestation of the five powers: first, the power of faith; second, the power of vigor; third, the power of mindfulness;
fourth, the power of concentration; and fifth, the power of wisdom. Therefore, it is said that one purifies the five eyes and attains the five powers.

Regarding the statement, "Only through realization can one know that which is difficult to fathom," this dharma-gate of the mind-ground must be personally realized in order to be known. It is like a person...
When drinking cold or warm water, one knows it for oneself; thus, it cannot be measured by means of conceptual thought. As the Sūtra says:
"If one attempts to measure the Tathāgata’s realm of perfect enlightenment with a mind of discursive thought, it is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly's glow;
even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would never catch fire. Therefore, it is said: "Only through realization can it be known; it is difficult to fathom."
It is not difficult to see one’s form in a mirror; but who can grasp the moon caught in water?
Although the form within the mirror may be seen, the moon in the water cannot be seized.

This is because worldly people turn their backs on this enlightened nature and instead identify with its reflections, drifting through birth and death, emerging and submerging, deeply attached [to appearances].
One cannot escape from external objects. Thus, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* says:

"For example, on a clear night, a troop of monkeys by a tree near a well suddenly sees the reflection of the moon. They immediately descend into the well one after another, attempting to grasp the moon;
yet they can never succeed in obtaining it. This is truly because all sentient beings follow after external conditions, and thus desire to return to their original source."
It is also like this; hence it is said, "Who can grasp the moon in the water?
He always walks alone, he always strides alone.
One who has realized the Dharma does not take the myriad dharmas as companions. Transcending the three realms, he strides alone through the Great Square. Therefore...
It is said: "One constantly walks alone. Those who have not yet attained realization have, throughout immeasurable kalpas, been in constant opposition to the various sense objects.

Having become deluded regarding the nature of awakening, they are deeply attached to the conditions of sensory objects; thus, from moment to moment, they are unable to abandon them. Therefore, a sutra says:
The eye-faculty perceives forms; the ear discriminates sounds; the nose smells various fragrances; the tongue licks at tastes;
the body-faculty greedily receives all tactile objects; and the mind-faculty discriminates all phenomena.
How could one possibly sever the past and future limits to walk alone and stride forth independently?
"Those who have attained [enlightenment] travel together on the road of *nirvāṇa*.
'Those who have attained' refers to those who have realized the Dharma. 'Nirvāṇa' means neither arising nor ceasing. 'Nir' (nirvana) signifies non-arising; 'vāṇa' (pāna) signifies non-ceasing.
This is the path of non-birth. As the Sūtra says: 'The Bhagavans of the ten directions [travel] upon one single path.'"
Nirvāṇa: this single path can only be traversed step by step upon the stages of the Buddha by those who have clarified the mind and realized the inherently present Mahāyāna lineage.
One must know that the three fruits are vast and the six realms are boundless;
all are people who have lost their way. For this reason, the thousand sages appeared in the world for the sake of the one great matter.
He urged you all to travel this path together, but from that time on, none of you were willing. As the ancient masters said:
"Thorns grow upon the road to heaven; the ground before the gates of hell is as slippery as moss. It may be said that few people tread upon it.
His tuning is ancient and his spirit is pure; his style rises naturally on high. His appearance is haggard and his bones are firm, so people pay him no heed.
Those who have not yet realized the Way are deeply attached to worldly conditions; their tastes are frivolous and gaudy, and their spirits are clouded and disordered.

When one loses what they guard within, they are no longer practitioners of the Way, regardless of whether they are active or still. A man of the Way is unstained by worldly conditions; his tuning and rhythm are ancient.
"Serene. His spirit was clear and refreshing, and his countenance bore the air of the Way. Thus it is said: "The melody is ancient and the spirit is pure; the wind naturally rises high.

As for "his appearance was haggard and his bones were rigid, so that people paid him no heed": although the great practitioner’s physical form was withered and emaciated, his mind was free from greed and desire.
Having mastery within, he was as firm and unyielding as metal or stone, yet few people recognized him. This was the case among the people of Jambudvīpa.
Deeply attached to the marks of form, they transmigrate through birth and death with no prospect of escape, yet fail to awaken.
For this reason, the Sage assumes the appearance of a poor man, remaining hidden within the world so as to be unfathomable.

Thus we know that those who follow the Way according to their fundamental nature harbor *prajñā* within and do not concern themselves with ornamental finery; their appearance is pure and ancient, such that few people recognize them. Hence it is said: "The appearance..."
A person with emaciated bones and a stern demeanor is not looked upon [with favor].
This destitute śrāmaṇera claims to be poor in speech, yet in reality it is his body that is poor while the Way is not poor.
Because a person who possesses the Way does not rely on external adornments, he is called "poor. An ancient sage said: "In studying the Way, one solemnizes the three [aspects of self]."
"Always insufficient"—is this not what that refers to? As for the term "Śākya-putra," it is a title received from the Buddha;
in full, one should say "of the Śākya clan," which is one of the five castes. When our Buddha was a crown prince during his causal stage, the king had four sons who were all exiled by the king.
These four princes converted people through their virtue, and they became powerful states. Their father—

The King, filled with regret, recalled his previous decree and dispatched messengers to summon them back. The four sons declined the summons and did not return. Their father, the King, sighed and said, "My son is a Śākya.
This is the Chinese translation for "Capable Benevolence" (Néngrén). Now, when one says "Śi" instead of "Śākyamuni," it is for the sake of brevity.

"Son" (zi) is a general term for a male; thus, they are called "Śākya Sons" (Shízǐ). As for those who call themselves "poor," although their mouths— (Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
He is called "poor," yet internally he harbors the noble Dharma; in truth, he is not poor. "In truth" refers to words that are ultimate reality.

One who is poor in body lacks worldly wealth, such as the seven treasures and so forth. One who is not poor in the Way—were one to discuss his Way—possesses immeasurable Dharma-wealth of virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which is inexhaustible in use.
Thus, although he has not even enough space to stick a needle upright, he is not poor in the Way.
In truth, this is worth as much as the Sahā world. Therefore it is said: "In truth, my body is poor, but my Way is not poor. The following passage clarifies this point.
Being "poor" means that one's body is constantly clad in coarse hempen garments; yet the "Way" means that within the mind is stored a priceless treasure.
To be poor means that one’s person lacks adornment; this is what is called poverty of the body. Yet, as for the Way, it is worthy of honor and esteem, and is truly not poor.
As an ancient sage said: "When the *kāṣāya* is torn, patch it layer upon layer; when there is no food at hand, provide for it bit by bit."
For this reason, Kāśyapa wore robes made of discarded rags, and the Buddha praised them as the supreme garments for spiritual practice;
he did so because moderation in food and frugality in clothing constitute contentment. As for the "priceless treasure stored within the mind" on the Path:
among the seven worldly treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, mother-of-pearl, pearl, and agate—all possess a specific value, whereas only the mind...
Because it is a treasure, it is priceless. Dharma said: "Among all phenomena, the mind-phenomenon is supreme; among all treasures, the mind-treasure is supreme.
This treasure has no form, and it is difficult to perceive at first glance unless one possesses the eye of the Way.
Therefore, it is called the 'priceless jewel hidden within.'"
Priceless treasure, inexhaustible in use; benefiting beings in accordance with conditions, it is never begrudged.
To speak again of "priceless treasure" clarifies that this jewel is truly not a worldly treasure. Regarding "inexhaustible in use":
all worldly treasures have limits; their use is always finite. Even if one’s lifespan were equal to that of Pengzu...
(One who preserves it for eight hundred years). In wealth, one is like Shi Chong (a person of peerless nobility). This is the glory of a lifetime;
yet only this treasure of the mind is inexhaustible in its use. From the Buddhas of the ten directions upward, even after passing through immeasurable kalpas, they never exhaust its enjoyment.
The twenty-eight patriarchs of the Western Heaven could not exhaust its use; the Sixth Patriarch of the Tang land could not exhaust its use;
the elder monks throughout the world could not exhaust its use; and even now, this mountain monk cannot exhaust its use.

"Benefiting beings by responding to conditions, never begrudging it"—on the crossroads of the city, he hands it over with full dignity; when has he ever been stingy? It is simply that people of the time...
Willingly accepting this, an ancient worthy said: "The pearl of the black dragon is not that which the black dragon begrudges; it is simply that people of the present age do not know how to seek it.
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfect within the essence; the eight liberations and six supernatural powers are the seal upon the ground of the mind."

The three bodies, four wisdoms, eight liberations, and six supernormal powers are named according to the functional manifestations of the awakened nature (*bodhi*). "Earth" (*bhūmi*) takes the sense of being able to give birth;
"seal" (*mudrā*) takes the sense of issuing commands. As for what are called the "three bodies": they are the *dharmakāya*, the *saṃbhogakāya*, and the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The "four wisdoms" are the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the Wisdom of Equality, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and [the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done].
This is the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Regarding the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*): first, the liberation through internal contemplation of forms;

second, the liberation through external contemplation of forms; third, the liberation of the pure sphere (*śubha-vimokṣa*); fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*); fifth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*).
Sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*). Seventh, the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*).
Eighth, the liberation of the ultimate cessation (*nirodha-dhātu-vimokṣa*). These eight liberations of the spheres are the eight liberations of consciousness.

Regarding what are called the eight consciousnesses: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind constitute the six consciousnesses; the seventh is the transmitting consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*); and the eighth is the *ālaya*, which is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Thus, the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms, and the four wisdoms are condensed into the three bodies (*trikāya*). Regarding the statement that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms:

the five consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); the sixth mental consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna*);

the seventh transmitting consciousness, the *manas*, is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*); and the eighth storehouse consciousness is transformed [into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom].
The ālayavijñāna is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Regarding the condensation of the four wisdoms into the three bodies (*trikāya*):

the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) constitute the Nirmāṇakāya; the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) is the Saṃbhogakāya;
and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the Dharmakāya. These three bodies are in fact but a single body. Do you wish to recognize this one body? It is the head that is round.
The Elephant Heaven: its feet are square like the earth; its ancient appearance is rugged and imposing, possessing the spirit of a great man.
A superior person, with a single resolution, understands everything; those of middle and lower capacity, despite much learning, possess little faith.
The unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma can be truly understood by the superior person (śreṣṭha-puruṣa) as soon as they hear it;
therefore, it is said that "the superior person, having made one decisive resolution, understands everything. Thus, when superior persons meet, the Way is present in their very gaze.

For those of middling and inferior capacity, much hearing only serves to increase their knowledge; hence it is said that "excessive words distance one further from the Way. Therefore, it is stated: "Those of middling and inferior capacity [rely on] much hearing."
Many do not believe this. Nevertheless, the same applies to all the verbal explanations found within the Three Teachings.
A Mahāyāna Bodhisattva attains great *dhāraṇī* upon hearing it once and awakening to a thousand truths; those of the various Hīnayāna schools are not capable of bearing this Dharma.
Laozi said: "The superior man, hearing the Way, practices it with diligence; the mediocre man, hearing the Way, is as if it exists and as if it perishes; the inferior man..."
When scholars hear this Way, they laugh at it loudly. If they did not laugh, it would not be worthy of being called the Way.
The *Zhuan* says: "If one can speak with someone, speak with them; if one cannot speak with someone, do not speak with them.

To speak with someone when one can speak with them is called 'missing the person'; to speak with someone when one cannot speak with them is called 'missing the words. Therefore, the poem by Hanshan says:
It is said: "The person of superior capacity has a sharp and keen mind; upon hearing once, they immediately know its subtlety. The person of middling capacity has a pure mind;
through careful reflection, they realize it is most essential. The person of inferior capacity is dull, dark, and deluded; their stubborn skin is most difficult to pierce.

Only when blood drenches their head do they finally realize they have destroyed themselves. Look at this 'open-eyed thief'—in the bustling marketplace, people decide [their fate]; a corpse is discarded like dust. This...
To whom, then, should one speak? A man, a true hero, cuts through with a single stroke.

When will the deeds of those with human faces but the hearts of beasts ever cease? Since the former sages have exhorted us in this way, those who possess roots of goodness will surely be moved upon hearing it.
One should simply remove the soiled garment from within one's own breast; who can boast of their diligence by looking outward?
"Soiled garment" refers to the afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā*). "Garment" has the meaning of covering; "soiled" means dust and defilement.
Dust has the meaning of staining and pollution. This ignorance is capable of covering over the pure Dharma.
The substance [of this] is able to defile the subtle and wondrous nature of awakening; therefore, it is likened to a soiled garment.

"Only one who unties the soiled garment from within their own bosom" means that this matter is one's own concern and cannot be performed by another. From the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) downward, all are Great Beings (*mahāsattva*) still wearing the soiled garment.
One who has seen the nature conceals and employs its mysteries, remaining unaffected by the afflictions of worldly dust.
It clarifies that which covers and obscures; thus it is said, "to shed the soiled garments. An ancient master said: "Cast off the greasy cap; strip away the stinking cloth tunic;
wave your hands and emerge from the thicket of thorns to attain great mastery. Those of the Hīnayāna focus exclusively on external phenomena;
though their bodies encircle the Dharma seat, their minds wander among the objects of perception. This is outward ostentation of diligence.
Master Bao said: "At the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.), when people are settled, even vigorous and diligent effort becomes indolence. This is precisely what he meant.
Let others slander; let others be wrong. To hold a torch and burn the sky is merely to exhaust oneself in vain.
To disparage and insult with words is called slander; to claim that what is right is wrong is called denial.

One who has realized their true nature remains tranquil in mind amidst all circumstances encountered throughout the twelve periods of the day, whether favorable or adverse, and is not turned by the myriad objects of perception.
Leave it to them to slander me as they please; since I do not accept it, the evil words and slanders will instead return to themselves.
It returns to oneself; that is to say, one reaps what one sows. It is like a person holding a fire-drill in their hand, intending to burn the heavens;
they will only exhaust themselves in vain, for it can never be achieved. Therefore, it is said: "To hold a torch and try to burn the heavens is but to weary oneself in vain."
When I hear [such words], it is as if I were drinking nectar; they melt away and enter suddenly into the inconceivable.
When I hear words of slander, it is as if I were drinking nectar; my mind becomes naturally cool and free from the fever of affliction.
When those who have not yet attained realization hear words of slander and dispute, their minds give rise to affliction;
it is as if they suddenly strike one place and flames erupt simultaneously in three places, impossible to extinguish. An ancient worthy said:
"The flower of awakening has seeds, but no one to sow them; the fire of the mind burns day after day without smoke. This is what is heard only by those who have realized their nature.
When one attains mastery of mind regarding words that are either contrary or conformable, one immediately enters the wondrous gate of inconceivable liberation; thus it is said:
"To dissolve and merge, entering suddenly into the inconceivable."
Contemplate this: malicious speech is itself a merit; it serves as my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When the ear hears malicious speech and no anger arises, one is immediately able to accomplish the power of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
One will not have the "six thieves" steal the family treasure; the wealth of the Dharma and merit will increase from this point on. Thus, one knows that such slander—

Such a person, in turn, becomes my virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). When it says "not hearing evil words but observing them," this refers to the mutual functioning of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
On the day my Buddha, the World-Honored One, attained enlightenment, the hosts of Māras contended against him.
Out of compassion for these beings, the Tathāgata entered the Samādhi of Loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*); at that time, the demonic hordes were ultimately unable to cause him harm.
This is the accomplishment of the merit of concentration and wisdom, adorned with myriad virtues.
Without giving rise to enmity or intimacy due to slander or defamation, how could this manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience?
If it were not for the slanderous and poisonous words of defamation directed at me from above, I would have realized that both good and evil reputations are ultimately ungraspable.
It is like the wind passing over the tops of trees; one hears only the sound, yet no distinction is made between the sounds of "good" or "evil.
Thus, I give rise to a mind of equanimity toward both enemies and kin, thereby accomplishing loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Regarding the four immeasurable minds of compassion, joy, equanimity, and [loving-kindness]:
when encountering circumstances that are either adverse or favorable during this time, one should remain with a mind of equality—serene, self-possessed, and free from all hindrance.
If one does not do so, how can one manifest the power of my path of non-arising compassion and patience?
The principle is also pervasive; the teaching is also pervasive.
The pervasiveness of the principle is precisely the pervasiveness of the Dharma. The Dharma is not verbal expression; verbal expression is not the Dharma. Yunmen said:
"When the carp of the Eastern Sea is struck with a single blow, the rain pours down like an overturned basin. Tianyi said: "This mountain monk rides backward upon the Buddha hall."
The various masters returned to wearing straw sandals; even Qingping leveled the earth, Guizong dragged stones, Deshan struck upon entering the gate, and Linji shouted upon entering the gate.
Regarding such acts of compassion as these, if one lacks the mind of awakening, how could one understand them?
One must directly and thoroughly clarify the fundamental principle and deeply penetrate the source; one must realize the essence right here and now, which is not the same as [ordinary understanding].

It is both perfect and gradual; therefore, it is called the "Penetration of the Essence" (*zongtong*). As for the "Penetration of the Teaching" (*shuotong*), this is the "Penetration of Meaning" (*yitong*):

being skillfully able to expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures, clearly elucidating their characteristics and categories, and knowing each one with complete understanding, free from doubt or error; therefore, it is called the "Penetration of the Teaching.

When it is now said that there is both penetration of the essence and penetration of the teaching, this refers to the dual penetration of both the Dharma and its meaning; one who is able to possess these—
Such individuals are extremely difficult to find. Those who are latecomers to this Dharma-gate do not understand its essential meaning and thus engage in mutual disputes of right and wrong.

As the tradition says: "In India, they divided the river and drank from separate streams; here in this land, Chan and Vinaya contradict one another. This is because both fail to clarify the two gates of Dharma and its meaning. Guifeng said:
"The Sūtras are like a carpenter’s line, used to determine what is deviant and what is correct. The line itself is not the skill; it is the one who uses it who possesses the skill."

The skillful must rely upon the plumb line and the carpenter’s square; yet the sutras and śāstras are not themselves meditation. Those who practice meditation must take the sutras and śāstras as their standard.
An ancient worthy said: "Those of today who study the ancient teachings cannot avoid mental agitation. To avoid mental agitation, one must indeed study the ancient teachings.
The tradition states: "The sutras are the Buddha’s words; meditation is the Buddha’s mind. Such is the mind of all Buddhas.
Their words shall certainly not contradict one another. The Great Master initially studied the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai Zhiyi;
later, having developed clear insight, he went to Caoxi to receive the seal of approval from the Sixth Patriarch. Thus, he profoundly clarified this essential principle; hence it is said:
"The school is thorough, and the teaching is thorough."
When concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are perfectly clear and bright, one does not stagnate in emptiness.

In the causal stage, these are called *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; in the resultant stage, they are called concentration and wisdom. The non-duality of concentration and wisdom is termed "perfect clarity.
This nature of perfect clarity is not the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the Hīnayāna; therefore, it is said that one does not stagnate in emptiness. This is truly because...
All sentient beings, from immeasurable kalpas past, have been intoxicated by ignorance and afflictions;

that they are unable to escape birth and death is solely due to the maladies of ignorance-induced dullness and distraction. Therefore, the Sages established the two dharmas of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight meditation) to treat them:
using *śamatha* to still distraction, so that amidst distraction there is tranquility; and using *vipaśyanā* to observe dullness, so that amidst dullness [there is clarity].

When this clarity is further developed, it transforms into the two dharmas of concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā). The non-duality of concentration and wisdom is called "perfect luminosity" (yuanming).
Perfect luminosity is a single dharma. This single dharma is the immeasurable merit and virtue of all Buddhas, an inexhaustible treasury of sublime functions.
All are enjoying this within the perfectly luminous Flower Treasury Ocean.
It is not that I alone have now attained realization; the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical.
Zhenjue himself said: "It is not only I who have now realized the aforementioned perfectly luminous Dharma-nature, even unto..."
The perfectly luminous essence of awakening of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is entirely the same. Therefore, a sutra says: "Not only do I know this mark;
the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise. As for the term "sands of the Ganges," it is named after a metaphor.
In India there is a river called the Gaṅgā. This river is forty li square, and within it there is sand as fine as flour.
The World-Honored One frequently used the sands of this river as a metaphor for the vast number of his teachings.
Now, Yongjia speaks in accordance with the sutras.
The lion’s roar is spoken without fear; when the hundred beasts hear it, their heads split open.
The lion is the king among beasts; when it lets out a single roar, the foxes vanish from sight, and all other animals flee in terror with their heads splitting apart.
This serves as a metaphor for the perfect and sudden Dharma-sound proclaimed by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas.
The palace of Māra trembled. Those whose vessels were of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) could not bear the Great Dharma; each gave rise to doubt and failed to awaken to understanding.
Thus, at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, they were as if deaf and mute, unable to believe or accept it.
Consider, for instance, when Deshan entered the gate and immediately struck with his staff, or Linji entered the gate and immediately shouted—how many could truly take this up?
The fragrant elephant rushes about, having lost its majesty; the devas and nāgas listen in silence, giving rise to joy.
The "fragrant elephant" is a metaphor for those of fixed nature among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas of the Hīnayāna, who are unable to turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna.

Because they could not sincerely believe in the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna they had heard, five thousand people left their seats and departed after bowing to the Buddha at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is like a king of elephants who, despite possessing majestic power, loses his majesty and flees as soon as he hears the lion’s roar;
thus it is said that "the fragrant elephant bolts away, losing its majesty. When the devas and nāgas listen in silence, they give rise to joy.
"Joyful" means that when the devas and nāga kings hear the lion’s roar, their hearts become glad and delighted.
This is a metaphor for those Mahāyāna bodhisattvas who, upon hearing the Great Dharma spoken by the Buddha, experience immeasurable joy and exultation in their hearts.
It is like Subhūti in the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, who rejoiced upon hearing the Buddha’s exposition of the *prajñā*.
This refers to the most profound compassion. Thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "At that time, Subhūti shed tears and wept as he addressed the Buddha, saying:
'It is rare, World-Honored One! From the past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard such a sūtra as this.
This is precisely its meaning."
I traveled across rivers and seas, traversed mountains and valleys, seeking teachers and inquiring after the Way to practice Zen.
My journeying through rivers and seas and my crossing of mountains and valleys—though the roads were wearying and I hurried back and forth between north and south—were not for any other purpose.

Rather, they were for the sake of seeking out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to resolve the matter of life and death. This is what is meant by the swift and sudden nature of impermanence and birth-and-death.
The matter is great. Ancient Touzi said: "All worldly people treat urgent matters as leisurely and treat leisurely matters as urgent.
If you wish to transcend birth and death, you must encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to serve as a superior condition (adhipatipratyaya)."
To clarify one's own fundamental matter is truly no small matter. As it is said, "The green mountains remain forever, yet those who possess true knowledge are hard to meet.
Therefore, it is stated that seeking a teacher and visiting the Way constitutes the practice of Chan meditation.
"Since I recognized the path of Caoxi, I have known that birth and death are not interconnected.

Since he went to Caoxi to receive the Sixth Patriarch’s certification in the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground, he has known that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing, and without coming or going. If one awakens to this Dharma-gate, then one will realize the original nature.
Life and death do not interfere with one another; thus it is said that one thoroughly understands that life and death are unrelated.
If one attains such a state, the wondrous function is inexhaustible and the entire body responds to things. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; speaking or remaining silent;
acting or performing; moving or gesturing; extending or contracting; bending or looking up—all these activities are none other than the clear and manifest enjoyment within great, tranquil samādhi.
This can be seen in the following passage:
"Walking is Zen; sitting is Zen. Whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, the essence remains serene.
Under the gate of our ancestors, every point provides instruction, and every beat reveals it clearly. As the Transmission says: "In every thought-moment, Śākyamuni appears."
In every step throughout the world, Maitreya descends to be born; in every discernment, he manifests the mind of Mañjuśrī;
in every movement and function, he carries out the conduct of Samantabhadra. In every gate, nectar flows forth; in every flavor, there is nothing but the finest essence (*sarpis*).

Without departing from the grove of Bodhi, one dwells eternally within the ocean of Flower Treasury (*Puṣpa-garbha-lokadhātu*). Radiant and brilliant, there is no dust that is not permeated; morning after morning...
Radiance overflows the eyes and brilliance surges forth; what need is there to labor with subtle eloquence to proclaim it, or to rely on supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to manifest it?

If this is so, then whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, whenever one encounters objects or conditions, although the applications may differ in a thousand ways, the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) remains profoundly still and unmoving.
Thus it is said: "Walking is Zen, sitting is Zen; speaking and silence, movement and stillness—the essence [is one]."
Tranquil and at ease.
Even if one encounters a sharp blade, one remains ever composed; even if one is given lethal poison, one remains relaxed.
Since throughout the twelve periods of the day both movement and stillness are acts of Buddha-work, even if someone were to take a sharp blade or poison...
If Bhaiṣajyarāja and I were added to this assembly, we would be at ease and leisurely, free from all fear.
Thus, in the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were five hundred bhikṣus who had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Using their knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), each of them observed their own past actions, such as killing their fathers, killing their mothers, and other grave offenses. Consequently, within their own minds, each harbored doubts and fears. Regarding this—
Mañjuśrī, wielding a sword, threatened and coerced the Tathāgata. The World-Honored One said to Mañjuśrī: "Stop, stop!
You must not commit an act of rebellion. Do not harm me. If I am to be harmed, let it be for the sake of goodness. Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning there has been no self or person;
it is only because of the internal mind that one perceives a self or person. When the internal mind arises—"
"If I am certainly being harmed, then that is what is called 'harm. The five hundred bhikṣus realized for themselves that their original mind is like a dream and like an illusion;
within this dream and illusion, there is no self or person, nor even parents who give birth or are born from them.
Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus praised him with one voice, saying: "Mañjuśrī, Great Sage of Wisdom, you have profoundly penetrated the source of all dharmas."
At the bottom [of the pit], he personally grasped a sharp sword and pressed it against the body of the Tathāgata. As the sword is, so too is the Buddha;
they are of one mark and have no duality. Being without marks and without arising, how could there be killing therein?
Tianyi asked, "How do you explain the saying, 'As the sword is, so too is the Buddha'? If one understands this causal condition, then even if one encounters a sharp blade, [one remains unharmed].
Always serene. Even if it were potent poison, it would be met with equanimity.
My Master beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; for many kalpas he was once the Immortal of Forbearance.
It is not only I who now cultivate this forbearance; even all the Buddhas of the ten directions, including Śākyamuni Tathāgata, have done so.
All of them practiced this asceticism of patience. As for the one called Dīpaṃkara Buddha:
when the World-Honored One was a youth on the Snowy Mountains during his causal stage, he encountered the appearance in the world of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.

He personally purchased lotus flowers with five hundred gold coins and went to offer them to that Buddha, vowing, "May I attain equal and perfect enlightenment. Then, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara conferred upon him [the prediction].
The Record states: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni. You shall preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings no differently than I have.
Thus it is said that my teacher met Dīpaṃkara Buddha. As for the Ascetic of Forbearance:
when the World-Honored One was on the path of practice as the Ascetic of Forbearance, he was dwelling in the mountains cultivating various ascetic practices when he encountered King Kaliṅga.
Accompanied by his court ladies, the king entered the mountains for a hunt. While the king was sleeping during the day, the ladies each went off to roam the mountains.
Suddenly, they saw an immortal sitting solemnly and alone within a hermitage. The ladies all came together to gaze upon him in reverence.
When the king arose, he asked his attendants, "Where are the ladies? His retinue replied, "They have gone to that place where the immortal is."
This was the hermitage. The king, enraged, personally drew his sword and slew that seer, dismembering him limb by limb from his hands and feet.
At that time, the seer’s countenance remained unmoved. The king, finding this strange, asked:
"Now that I have killed you, do you still feel anger? He replied: "No. The king said: "Though you do not speak of it, you must surely harbor anger. He replied: [No.]
He said, "If my mind were to harbor anger, it could not be restored to its natural state. Since my mind is free from anger, let this body of mine be restored as it was before.
As soon as he had finished speaking, the rishi immediately recovered as he had been. When the king saw this extraordinary marvel, he fled in terror.
On the way, a storm of wind and rain, thunder, and mist descended from the heavens; he lost his way and ultimately did not [reach his destination].
He was able to depart and return to the mountains to seek out the rishi and beg for forgiveness.

He even went so far as to sacrifice his body to feed a starving tigress and cut off his own flesh to relieve the hunger of a hawk; such various ascetic practices had been performed by him not merely for a single kalpa.
Therefore, it is said that over many kalpas he was once the Rishi Kṣāntivādin (the Rishi of Forbearance).
"How many times born? How many times dead? Birth and death drift on endlessly, with no fixed end.
These are words of lamentation from True Awakening (Zhengjue). Prior to the arousal of the Bodhicitta, one undergoes immeasurable lifetimes throughout countless kalpas;
within the ocean of birth and death, the waves rise and fall of their own accord without end. Regarding this—
Transmigrating through realms, they vainly undergo the cycle of saṃsāra; within a state where no dharma of liberation exists, they delusively give rise to fetters.
Like silkworms in spring spinning cocoons, or like moths in autumn rushing toward a lamp, they use the threads of dualistic views to entangle the substance of ignorance.
With the wings of ignorance and craving, one strikes against the fire-wheel of birth and death, proceeding from life to death without rest.
It is like a bird tied with a rope; though released, it returns again. Thus it is said: "How many times born, how many times dead?
Birth and death drift on endlessly, without fixed end."
Since awakening suddenly to non-arising, what cause for sorrow or joy can there be amidst all honors and insults?
Since one has suddenly awakened to the fact that all dharmas are entirely without arising, what sorrow or joy can there be regarding the conditions of honor and insult?
This is truly because the Perfected Person has attained mastery within the realm of birth and death; thus, [they remain unaffected by] cold...
A mountain poem says: "Zhuangzi spoke of sending off the end; heaven and earth serve as the outer and inner coffins. When my time to return here comes, I shall simply require one final mooring.
To die is to become food for the blue flies; there is no need for white cranes to offer condolences. One may starve upon Mount Shouyang."
One who lives with integrity finds joy even in death. If one grasps this essential meaning, one immediately awakens to the realization that there is no birth.
As for why one would have neither sorrow nor joy regarding various honors and insults: once one has attained immediate awakening to the absence of birth, one gains mastery over both life and death;
thus, one knows that the realms of honor and insult can be cast aside. When honor and insult are forgotten, from where could the mind of sorrow and joy arise?
There is. One enters deep mountains and dwells in an araṇya (hermitage) beneath tall, towering pines in a secluded and remote place.
"Entering deep mountains" means it is not a bustling or crowded location. "Dwelling in an araṇya" should be stated in its full form as follows:
"Āraṇya" refers to a monastic dwelling. "Steep peaks" describes the lofty appearance of mountains. "Beneath long pines" refers to a place of leisure beyond the mundane world.
One who has realized their nature passes the days according to conditions and roams freely as they please;
whether entering deep mountains or residing in rocky valleys, they establish themselves wherever they may be, responding to circumstances without fixed method—there is nothing they cannot do.
This is fitting. White clouds and green peaks, beneath pines and by watersides—these are all the realms of the wayfarer.
To wander at ease and sit in stillness within the home of a wild monk, to dwell in profound tranquility—this is truly refined and elegant.
"Leisurely and unhurried" (*youyou*) describes a state of being unbound and unconstrained. Those who have left the household life recognize the mind and penetrate the fundamental source;

they move with ease through the three realms and cast off the four modes of birth. Unfettered by the entanglements of worldly toil, they roam at will in sovereign freedom, dwelling in tranquil stillness.
Thus Xuedou said: "The one who has left the household life attains such nobility, attains such loftiness. Ten thousand...
Though occupying a high station, he does not pride himself; though the gates of the Five Marquises are steep, he does not hasten toward them.
Before his eyes lie a thousand mountains, yet his mind rests in a single realm of tranquility. Layer upon layer, the trees on the crags cast their shade over the gate of Saṃjaya;
tier upon tier, the clouds over the stream spread their colors within the chamber of Vimalakīrti. To meet one another here—how joyful this is!
Awakening is realization; it requires no effort. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are distinct;
yet, when one awakens to all dharmas, one does not exert effort in conditioned practices.
Conditioned effort is not ultimate. Thus, Hanshan said: "I see the Wheel-Turning King, constantly surrounded by his thousand sons. [He practices] the ten virtues..."
They transform the four heavens, adorning them with many of the seven treasures; these seven treasures remain constantly with them, their adornment most exquisite and wonderful.

Yet when the retribution of their merit is exhausted in a single morning, they are like birds perching upon reeds; they return to become insects on a bull's neck, undergoing the paths of karma within the six realms of existence.
How much more so for ordinary worldlings—how could impermanence ever be long preserved?

By this one may know that the merit of meritorious deeds is all impermanent, whereas the merit of non-meritorious deeds is not wasted in vain. Therefore it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are not the same.
Giving with attachment to signs produces the merit of rebirth in heaven, which is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void.
One who gives with attachment to signs does not accord with *prajñā*; because they are attached to signs, their meritorious practice becomes conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and is not ultimate.
Thus, an ancient master said: "If *prajñā* is not cultivated, the myriad practices are established in vain. Regarding what is cultivated...
Merit and practice cannot fully correspond to the nature [of reality]. As for what is called "giving" (dāna): to extend the mind broadly is termed "spreading" (bu);
to push oneself aside to benefit others is termed "bestowing" (shi). Hence it is called "giving" (dāna). It is one of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
Regarding those who attain the merit of rebirth in heaven: the retribution they experience is merely the merit of being born in heaven; it is ultimately not final.
It is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the sky; it will never reach heaven [permanently].
When its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down; it brings about an unfavorable rebirth in the next life.
Just as an arrow shot upward into the sky inevitably falls to the ground once its force is spent, so too is it with the exhaustion of merit in the human and celestial realms.
This refers to the four signs of decay in the human world and the five signs of decline in the heavens, all of which are manifestations of the waning of merit. As it is said:
The four signs are: first, the sign of birth; second, the sign of aging; third, the sign of illness;
and fourth, the sign of death. The five signs of decline are: first, the flower crown falls to the ground; second, the eyelashes twitch; third, one’s retinue disperses;

fourth, the bodily radiance naturally extinguishes; and fifth, one finds no pleasure in one’s own seat. Regarding that which brings about an unfavorable rebirth in a future life, an ancient master said: "A person..."
Heavenly rewards of fortune become the cause for enmity in three lifetimes; few people understand this.
It is because worldly beings, relying on the power of their merit, fail to clarify its fundamental nature and instead add further to it.

They indulge their passions and enjoy themselves with these worldly blessings, yet at the moment of death, when the merit is exhausted and karma remains, they fall back into the evil realms to undergo various sufferings. Therefore, it is said that one "summons" [retribution] for the next life.
This is not as one would wish.
How can it compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark (asamskṛta-lakṣaṇa), which transcends in a single leap directly into the stage of the Tathāgata?
Thus, one should know that all the conditioned dharmas—the various stages of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, humans, and devas, as well as their meritorious retributions—are ultimately not final.
How can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark, which transcends all at once to enter directly into the Tathāgata’s ground of pure awakening?
This single path has never been trodden by the thousand sages of antiquity; here, within the second gate, I shall briefly rely upon words and explanations.
Therefore, the First Patriarch of India said: "The Dharma is originally without Dharma; the absence of Dharma is itself Dharma.

Now, when transmitting the state of no-Dharma, how could any phenomenon ever have been a phenomenon? Thus, all phenomena are free from mutual dependence; they are entirely the independent manifestation of the luminous essence.
Just as a finger cannot touch itself, as a sword cannot cut itself, as the earth cannot be hard by itself,
as water cannot be moist by itself, as fire cannot be hot by itself, as wind cannot move by itself, as the ear cannot hear itself, as the nose cannot smell itself,
as the tongue cannot taste itself, as the body cannot feel itself, and as the mind cannot know itself, so it is with the eye.
One does not see for oneself. Therefore it is said: "If the eye produces the cognition of 'eye,' then the inversion of the eye arises.
If the eye produces the cognition of 'no-eye,' then the inversion of no-eye arises. If one clings to the existence of the eye, one is deluded regarding its non-existence.
Because of the existence of the eye, wondrous vision is obstructed. Thus the Sūtra says: "There is neither eye nor form," yet there is further delusion that takes the eye to be non-existent.
Those with eyes lose their true vision; they are like those born blind who cannot distinguish colors. Thus the Sūtra says:
"For example, a man whose eyes have been destroyed can no longer perceive the five colors. The śrāvakas are likewise;
only the Tathāgata possesses the true divine eye, which is ever-present and never obscured, seeing all the Buddha-lands."

Because he views through non-duality, he does not share the perspective of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); because he is able to see all that is seen, he does not share the perspective of the *śrāvakas*.
That his vision differs from what is seen by ordinary beings is called "transcending the ordinary"; that it differs from what is seen by the *śrāvakas* is called "surpassing the sages.
Being thus able to transcend both the ordinary and the sage, he attains the knowledge and vision of the Buddha; hence it is said:
This is to leap directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
Simply attain the root; do not worry about the branches. It is like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon:
