Shu transmitted [the lineage] to the fifteenth patriarch, Kāṇadeva; Deva transmitted it to the sixteenth patriarch, Rāhulata;
Tata transmitted it to the seventeenth patriarch, Saṃghanandin; Nandin transmitted it to the eighteenth patriarch, Gayāsata;
Sata transmitted it to the nineteenth patriarch, Kumāralata; Lata transmitted it to the twentieth patriarch, Jayata; and Jayata transmitted it to the twenty-first... [patriarch].
The first patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, transmitted it to the twenty-second patriarch, Maṇara; Maṇara transmitted it to the twenty-third patriarch, Haklena;
Haklena transmitted it to the twenty-fourth patriarch, Siṃha; Siṃha transmitted it to the twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasubandhu;
Vasubandhu transmitted it to the twenty-sixth patriarch, Kumārajīva; Kumārajīva transmitted it to the twenty-seventh...
The patriarch Prajñātāra transmitted it to the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma;
thus it is called the "Record of the Twenty-eight Generations in the Western Heaven.
Having traversed rivers and seas, he entered this land, with Bodhidharma serving as the First Patriarch.
In Sanskrit, he is called Bodhidharma; here it is translated as "Awakening to the Dharma. In Western India, he was the twenty-eighth patriarch;
in this land, he is the First Patriarch. He was originally the third prince of King Xiangzhi of South India.
Having encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, the patriarch, knowing his secret traces and having him realize the essential point of the mind, recorded for him: "You must not travel far yet."
Cease for now in Southern India. Wait until sixty-seven years after my parinirvāṇa; at that time, you shall go to China (Zhendan) and greatly propagate the Buddha’s work.
When you reach the south, do not remain; there, people cherish only conditioned achievements and do not perceive the principle of the Buddha.
Even if you should arrive there, you must not stay long. Listen to my verse: "Traveling along the road, crossing water, one encounters a sheep again. Alone..."
Alas, he crossed the river in silent sorrow. Beneath the setting sun, how pitiable were his two noble steeds; yet those two young cassia trees have long flourished in prosperity.
While the Master was in his own country, he used the power of his knowledge and vision to refute the divergent views of the six schools:

first, the School of Phenomenal Marks; second, the School of Non-Phenomenal Marks; third, the School of Samādhi and Prajñā; and fourth, the School of Precepts and Practice. The Dharma Master then caused them to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and return to the Great Vehicle.
The Five Non-Attainment schools and the Six Quiescence schools each clung to their own interpretations and separately expanded their sources of conversion;
their settlements were vast and their followers extremely numerous. The Great Master then sighed deeply and said:

"If even one of those teachers has already fallen into the tracks of an ox, how much more so these fragmented and proliferating groups that have split into six schools? If I do not eliminate them, they will forever entangle the world in heterodoxy."
He saw them; as each was told their own tenets, they realized individually that there was no place to turn for refuge. Only then did they return to the source and attain awakening.
The Master’s learning encompassed the Tripitaka, and he was especially devoted to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Those who were ignorant [of his depth] were cast aside.
The Master set sail from South India across the sea, traveling for three years. On the twenty-first day of the ninth month of the eighth year of the Putong era, he arrived at Guangzhou.
The Provincial Governor, Xiao Ang, memorialized Emperor Wu. Upon reading the petition, the Emperor dispatched an envoy bearing an imperial decree to invite him.

On the first day of the tenth month, he arrived in Jinling. When the Emperor invited him to the capital, he asked, "Since my accession to the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks beyond counting.
What merit do these deeds possess? The Master replied, "These are merely merits pertaining to the realm of humans and devas."
The causes for minor fruits and outflows follow their effects like a shadow follows a form; though they exist, they are not real. The Emperor asked, "What, then, are true merits?
The Master replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and still. Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means.
The Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Master replied, "Vast and open—there is no 'holy' one. The Emperor...
The Emperor asked, "Who is it that faces me? The Master replied, "I do not know. The Emperor failed to grasp the meaning.

Realizing that the occasion was not one for harmony, the Master secretly returned north of the Yangtze River on the nineteenth day of that month. On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, he arrived at Luoyang.
This was later, in the tenth year of the Dahe era of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty.
He resided at Shaolin on Mount Song, sitting facing a wall and remaining silent throughout the day; no one could fathom him. He was the First Patriarch of the Chan school.
"The transmission of the robe through six generations is renowned throughout the world; the number of later followers who attained the Way is beyond measure.
Since the Great Master had not yet found one who understood him after nine years at Shaoshi, there was at that time a monk named Shen Guang, a man of vast and open spirit.
Having long resided in the Yi and Luo regions, he had widely read many books and was skilled in discussing the profound principles of the Way. He often sighed, saying: 'Confucius...'"
The teachings of Laozi on ritual arts and social norms, and the books of Zhuangzi and Yi Jing, have not yet exhausted the wondrous principles.

Recently, I heard that the Great Being Bodhidharma was residing at Shaolin. Since this sage is not far away, I should surely seek the profound realm. Thus, I went there to attend upon him morning and evening;
however, the Master sat upright facing a wall, and I heard no words of instruction or encouragement. Huiguan reflected to himself: "In the past, people sought..."
The Way! To beat the bones to extract the marrow; to pierce the flesh to provide sustenance for the hungry; to spread one's hair to cover the mud; to throw oneself from a cliff to feed a tiger.
If the ancients were such as this, what person am I? On the ninth night of the twelfth month of that year, it rained and snowed heavily.

Daguang stood firm and unmoving. By the time dawn arrived, the accumulated snow had reached above his knees. The Master, moved by pity, asked him: "Why have you been standing in the snow for so long?"
"What do you seek within this? Guang replied with tears of sorrow, "I only pray that the Master, out of compassion, will open the gate of ambrosia to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
The Master said, "The unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort through vast eons;
one must perform what is difficult to perform and endure what is difficult to endure. How can you hope for the True Vehicle with such meager virtue and wisdom, or with a frivolous and arrogant mind?"
In vain he exerted himself with toil and hardship. Upon hearing his master’s exhortation, Guang secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the master.
Recognizing him as a vessel for the Dharma, the master said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot their very forms for the sake of the Dharma."
"You have now severed your arm before me; your request may indeed be granted. He then changed his name to Huìkě.
Dàoguāng asked, "May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? The Master replied, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another. Dàoguāng said:
"My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. The Master said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall grant you peace.
Huiguan said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is ultimately unobtainable. The Master said, "I have finished granting you peace.

Having attained awakening through this, he became the Second Patriarch. As for what is called the transmission of the robe through six generations, since the Second Patriarch received it from the First Patriarch, they all...
The robe and alms bowl were transmitted from one to another. The First Patriarch personally transmitted the robe to the Eastern Land from Western India to manifest his seal of faith.
By the time it reached the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, the Way had already been established; thus, he no longer transmitted the robe, transmitting only the Dharma. Bodhidharma transmitted it to Huike;
Huike transmitted it to Sengcan; Sengcan transmitted it to Daoxin; Daoxin transmitted it to Hongren; and Hongren transmitted it to Huineng—Huineng being the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi.
He was a Great Master whose Way flourished widely throughout the world; it is said that the transmission of the robe through six generations was known by all under heaven.

Since then, those who have attained the Way have been beyond counting. Thus it is said that those who have become Buddhas and Patriarchs cover the earth and fill the heavens, while those who practice Chan and study the Way are as numerous as hemp and millet. Therefore, it is said that the number of later followers who attain the Way is inexhaustible.
Thus, the true does not establish itself; the false is fundamentally empty. Both existence and non-existence are discarded, yet it is neither empty nor non-empty.

Since the true does not establish itself, the false is likewise fundamentally empty. This is because both the true and the false originally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they arise dependent upon the true.
Falsity. Because of falsity, truth is established. An ancient master said: "A solitary truth cannot be established; a lone falsity is difficult to form.
Regarding the simultaneous negation of both existence and non-existence: existence and non-existence are also established in mutual dependence. Now that both are negated, even emptiness is empty.
Therefore, it is said that both existence and non-existence are simultaneously discarded; this is the emptiness of emptiness.

These several phrases were employed by the Great Master because he wished to reveal his Dharma, and thus he simultaneously brought forth the conditions of both the true and the delusive, as well as existence and non-existence.
The twenty gates of emptiness are fundamentally unattached; the single nature of the Tathāgata’s essence is inherently identical.
Regarding the "twenty gates of emptiness": the Tathāgata refuted twenty kinds of views that cling to existence, and thereby established the names of the twenty emptinesses.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "That is to say, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness..."

The emptiness of the great, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of the absolute limit, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless,

the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, the emptiness of self-characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility,
the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. Although there are these twenty names for emptiness, their...
The essence is precisely the One Dharma. Now, it is clarified that the principle of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) differs from the twenty kinds of emptiness;

therefore, it is said that "from the beginning, it is unattached. As for "the essence of the single nature and the Tathāgata are inherently identical," this means they transcend the sixty-two types of divergent views of the non-Buddhists and are in profound accord with the wondrous mind of *prajñā-nirvāṇa*; hence, it is said that "their essence is inherently identical."
The mind is the root; phenomena are the dust. These two are like blemishes upon a mirror. Regarding "the mind is the root":
"root" (mūla) takes the sense of being that which can produce. It is because this mind can produce all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas that it is called the "root.
Regarding "phenomena are the dust": although phenomena are able to serve as the standard and support for all things, they are nevertheless...
It is like a potent medicine: once the illness has been cured, the medicine is necessarily of no further use. Thus, dharmas are but dust.
These two types of phenomena both create obstructions, preventing the light of the human mind from penetrating through, much like a blemish upon a mirror.
Therefore it is said: when the sense faculties and their objects interact, they obscure the light of the mind. To return to the source and clarify the mind, this is precisely why.
Once the scars and impurities are entirely removed, the light finally appears; when both mind and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished, the nature is truly real.
If stains and defilements are exhausted, both mind and dharmas vanish together; naturally, the light of the mind penetrates through, and one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature.
As an ancient worthy said: "When a single film is in the eye, empty flowers fill the world; when a single delusion is in the mind, the sands of the Ganges arise and perish."
When the cataract is cleared and the flowers vanish, delusion is extinguished and reality is realized. When the illness is cured, the medicine is discarded; when the ice melts, the water remains.
A single grain of elixir can transform iron into gold; a single word of ultimate truth can turn an ordinary person into a sage. Therefore, it is said that "nature is itself reality."
"Alas for the Final Dharma! Alas for this evil age! Sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline. "Alas" (*jia*) is a word of lamentation.
When the World-Honored One appeared in the world and turned the Great Wheel of Dharma, he benefited sentient beings.

The True Dharma (*saddharma*) lasted for one thousand years; the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*) lasted for one thousand years; and the Final Dharma (*antarmārga*) lasts for ten thousand years. The Great Master’s appearance in the world coincided precisely with [the period of] the Final Dharma.
Regarding the Semblance Dharma, one has long lamented it as being such; this can be known even now. Thus it is said: "Alas for the Final Dharma!
In this evil age, the merit of sentient beings is meager and they are difficult to discipline. In the final age, the propagation of the Way does not clarify the Great Principle;
each school guards its own gate and courtyard, stubbornly adhering to its own views. These are all considered maladies of the Dharma, as can be seen in the following text.
"The Sage has long departed and false views have deepened; Mara is strong while the Dharma is weak, resulting in much resentment and harm.
The Sage having been far removed for a long time, false views have grown increasingly profound, such that people instead give rise to resentment and malice toward the True Dharma.

For this reason, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he struck his teeth to prove his innocence and endured poison. If even the Holy Master was thus treated, how much more so the human teacher? When the Buddhas appear in the world...

In this world, there is none who does not give rise to compassion and extend pity to embrace sentient beings and benefit their lives. Yet, even when Māra is powerful and the Dharma is weak, such beings remain unaware of the kindness and virtue of the Sages.
How much more so now, when the world has enjoyed peace for a long time, and kings and ministers, having received the Buddha’s entrustment, extensively protect the Triple Gem;
and when the assemblies of the various Dharma masters flourish, those who have left the household life ought to recognize the rarity of this opportunity.
With such a mind, one should seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to resolve the matter of birth and death, seeking liberation therefrom and repaying the four debts of gratitude;
this is what is appropriate. Nevertheless, among them, there are those who, though they study the Buddha-dharma, do not know of the "separate transmission outside the teachings.
There are also those who, occupying positions of high rank, forget the practices cultivated in their past lives regarding the Buddha-dharma.
There are indeed those who act as obstacles to this. There are also those who, though they uphold the Buddha-dharma, attack one another because their respective schools and lineages differ.
These are all demonic activities within the Dharma-gate; none of them are people of universal understanding.
If one were a person of true fundamental capacity, they would certainly not act in such a way. Thus, Guifeng said: "The various schools..."

Within our school there have always been men of great attainment; yet each remains settled in their own habitual studies. Those who possess broad understanding are few, while those who are narrow and limited are many.
They take what they have inherited as their windows and doors, each opening out in their own direction; they take the sūtras and śāstras as their weapons, attacking one another.

Their sentiments shift like the movement of arrows and halberds, and the Dharma rises or falls according to the person. Consequently, right and wrong become entangled in confusion, such that no one can resolve them.
Through such analysis, it is said that "the māras are strong and the Dharma is weak, and there are many enmities and harms.
Upon hearing the teaching of the Tathāgata’s sudden (sudden-enlightenment) gate, they harbor resentment, failing to extinguish it and instead seeking to smash it to pieces like broken tiles.

The Tathāgata has appeared in the world for the sole purpose of the one great matter. In this world there is a Māra King who, though contemporary with the Buddha, does not believe in the existence of the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate.
Hearing what the Buddha teaches, he slanders it all, lamenting that he cannot destroy it until it is shattered like a broken tile.
Furthermore, as for those people in the world who either possess or lack the capacity for the Mahāyāna, he likewise [does not believe].

There are those who possess the capacity for awakening and entry into the Dharma-gate; yet, though they have physically left the household life within the Śākya tradition, they still lack faith themselves.
Thus, such people exist. As the ancient masters said: "One must not speak of the absence of flowers in the sky before one whose eyes are clouded by cataracts;
one must not speak of the absence of ghosts before one who is suffering from madness. Such empty words will be met with non-belief and non-acceptance.
You must simply purify your vision and settle your mind; then you shall know for yourself.
What is done resides in the mind, and the retribution falls upon the body. There is no need to harbor resentment or blame others.
The immeasurable and boundless karma created by worldly people is all produced by the deluded mind; therefore it is said that "what is done resides in the mind."
It is the mind that brings about immeasurable bitter fruits: various forms such as those of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, who undergo manifold sufferings.
As the ancient masters said: "Who is it that comes bearing the saddle and mouthing the iron bit? It was simply because of past errors in the workings of the mind.
Thus it is said, "Calamity rests upon oneself"; all this is what one has done and must receive for oneself, not brought about by others. Therefore...
It is said that one need not lodge grievances or place blame upon others. The sufferings of the world last but a single lifetime, whereas the sufferings of hell are without end.
There are various unspeakable torments, such as those of the Sword-Tree and the Knife-Mountain.

Once these have been fully experienced in this realm, when the world-system perishes, one moves on to another realm to undergo punishment in its hells. When that retribution is exhausted, one is reborn among the animals.
Neither the donkey nor the horse was anyone else; it was solely the result of one's own actions being experienced by oneself.
If you wish not to incur karma leading to the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
The sin of slandering the Dharma is no small transgression. Those who destroy the *prajñā* will all fall into hell; this is likewise not a minor calculation.
These hells are all the Avīci Hell, which is the most grievous of prisons. The duration of time is vast, measured in kalpas.
The retribution for slandering the Dharma is manifold, as fully recorded in the Tripiṭaka; for instance, one may become a nine-headed tortoise.
Or one may suffer from diseases such as white leprosy; this is truly because the Buddhas of the ten directions, upon appearing in the world, all praise the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle.
It is by realizing this Dharma that the Buddhas of the ten directions attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
To now turn back and slander it is a grave transgression; therefore, it is said: "Do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.
In a sandalwood forest there are no other trees; dense and deep, it is where the lion dwells.

The metaphor of the sandalwood forest represents the single, wondrous realm of ultimate truth (*tathatā*). "No mixed trees" means there is no admixture of small-capacity vehicles or provisional stages.
"Lush, dense, and deep-seated" describes its profuse growth; "lush and dense" refers to its flourishing appearance, while "deep-seated" refers to its profound and secluded nature.
"The lion dwells therein" serves as a metaphor for the realm of *dharmatā*, which is inhabited solely by Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.
Those of inferior capacity among humans and devas cannot understand this; thus we know that the unsurpassed Prajñāpāramitā only connects with those of superior faculties and superior status.
Those of middling or inferior capacity find it difficult to awaken and enter suddenly. Therefore it is said: "In a sandalwood forest there are no other trees;
dense, lush, and profound, it is the dwelling place of the lion."
In the tranquility of the forest, one wanders alone; beasts and birds alike flee far away.
The Unconditioned Great Way is trodden only by Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas; those of the various Hīnayāna vehicles and practitioners of provisional stages cannot set foot there.
The lion is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, while the beasts and birds are metaphors for [the others].
This refers to those of limited capacity among humans, devas, and the two vehicles. For this reason, the five thousand who withdrew from their seats in the *Lotus Sūtra* were not fit for this matter.
The single true, wondrous realm is frequented only by superior practitioners; it is difficult for those of middling or inferior capacities to suddenly grasp. Therefore, it is said:
Wandering alone in the quietude of the forest, the wild beasts and birds all fled far away.
As for the lion cub, though the pack followed behind him, at three years of age he was already able to let out a great roar.

What is called the "lion cub" is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva attaining equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) at the very moment of first generating the resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
Because he transcends the various followers of the Lesser Vehicle, such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is said that "the multitude follows behind him.

The "three years" represents the person who has realized their nature (*dṛṣṭa-svabhāva*) perfectly cultivating the three dharmas. The Wise One [Zhiyi] said: "Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the merging of the one..."
All phenomena are thus. "The provisional" (jia) establishes all phenomena. "The middle" (zhong) is the wondrous nature of all phenomena. Emptiness is not fixed as emptiness;
within the locus of emptiness, its very substance is the middle and the provisional. The provisional is not fixed as the provisional;

within the locus of the provisional, its very substance is emptiness and the middle. The middle is not fixed as the middle; within the locus of the middle, its very substance is emptiness and the provisional. This—
The three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor distinct. In a single place there are always three, and in three places there is always one.
Thus it is said: "The three truths, the three contemplations, and the three that are not three; the three, the one, and the one-three have no fixed locus.

While the names of the truths and contemplations differ, their essence is identical. Therefore, the duality of subject and object is non-dual. Those who awaken and enter this realization perfectly verify the three.
The Dharma: all the Dharma-gates he expounds are the Middle Way and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Therefore it is said that at three years of age he was already able to let out a great roar.
If it were a jackal chasing after the Dharma King, it would be a hundred-year-old monster vainly opening its mouth.
The jackal is a metaphor for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). The lion is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.

The Bodhisattva deeply awakens to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); from the very first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), they attain perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*), and all the Dharma-gates they teach are entirely in accord with that nature.
Those of the Two Vehicles, ordinary beings, and individuals at various provisional stages who are unable to clearly perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) are like the jackal.
What has been said does not clarify the principle of the ultimate true reality; it is like hundreds of thousands of demons opening their mouths in vain, ultimately providing no benefit.
Therefore, it is said: "Hundreds of thousands of demons open their mouths in vain."
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching (Yuantun jiao). Do not follow human sentiments. If there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must simply contend with it.
"Perfect" (yuan) means complete; "Sudden" (dun) is not gradual. "Teaching" (jiao) means emulation. The Sage has fully set forth the words below.

The principle of "interpreting and transforming phenomena" constitutes its meaning. The teaching of the Perfect and Sudden does not rely on gradual stages, but transcends directly into the realm of the Buddha.
As the transmission says: "It is like a crown prince who possesses the virtues of a king's righteousness, or like the kalaviṅka bird whose song surpasses that of all other birds."
"Do not harbor human sentiments. "Do not" here means "the multitude. If any sentient being has doubts that they cannot resolve, they must directly seek clarity.
This is not a worldly study; for the matter of birth and death is great and is truly no small matter.
Therefore, the following section clarifies its causes and effects.
"It is not that this mountain monk seeks to display the distinction between self and others; I fear that in my practice I might fall into the pit of nihilism or eternalism.
This was Yongjia’s own reflection. How could it be that this mountain monk harbors a mind of competitive self-aggrandizement?
It is rather out of deep concern for future generations that all sentient beings, when resolving to practice within the Dharma-gate, might mistakenly employ [their efforts].
The mind falls into the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. Because these two views can cause people to sink, they are called "pits," just like the pits and moats of the world.
Among the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) in India, none transcend these views;
thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Whether there is existence or non-existence, etc., by relying on these various views, one becomes fully possessed of the sixty-two [views]."
This is precisely its meaning.
It is not "not-not," nor is it "is-is. To err by even a hair's breadth is to lose one's way by a thousand li.
That which is "not-not" and "is-is" clarifies that the characteristics of right and wrong are distinct and must not be confused.
"Non" (fei) does not mean merely being non; it is true non. "Is" (shi) does not mean merely being is; it is true is.
Although thus there is no master over right and wrong, one must not deceive oneself regarding Buddha-nature or treat True Suchness (Tathatā) as a vague generality.

To err by the measure of a hair (maoli) is to lose the mark by a thousand li. A hair that grows from the fur is called *máo*; ten *máo* make one *háo*. *Máo* refers to the fine hairs on the body, while *háo* refers to the longer hairs.
If one errs by even a hair’s breadth, one will lose one’s way by a thousand or ten thousand *li*. Therefore, the following text deeply clarifies the distinction between right and wrong:
to be right is for the Dragon Girl to suddenly attain Buddhahood; to be wrong is for Śunakṣatra to fall into ruin.
The Dragon Girl and Sunakṣatra serve to clarify the characteristics of right and wrong. Long ago, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, a dragon girl offered a precious jewel to the Buddha.

The World-Honored One accepted it and preached the Dharma for her; she realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and immediately departed for the stainless world (*Vimalā-loka*) in the south, where she sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained perfect enlightenment, being named Huaxian (Flower-Fresh).
It is indeed the Tathāgata. If it were not so, how could Śunakṣatra have fallen into such ruin?
Formerly, there was a bhikṣu named Śunakṣatra who claimed to have mastered the eighteen *piṭakas* of the fragrant elephants; yet he fell alive into hell.
Because he failed to perceive the Buddha-nature and instead preached the Dharma in a manner that constituted slander and profanation, this serves as a solemn warning.
Since my youth, I have accumulated learning and inquiry; I have also investigated commentaries and sought out the sūtras and śāstras.
Now, wishing to clarify the merit of formlessness (animitta), I shall first clarify the principle of having form (sanimitta).

The Great Master, in his youth, frequented various lecture halls and listened to the collected teachings and contemplations of Tiantai Zhiyi; he was profoundly learned in the sūtras and śāstras, having accumulated study and engaged in extensive questioning.
The former masters said: "Before five summers have passed, one should diligently study the Vinaya and gain a clear understanding of the Sūtras and Śāstras;

only then should one seek out spiritual friends to resolve matters concerning birth and death. This is the sequence for entering the Way. Were it not for those who possess the seeds of the Mahāyāna and the power of past vows, it would be rare to fulfill this entirely.
Among the sages of antiquity, there were none who did not follow this path; even the Patriarch Bodhidharma was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka.

This is especially true regarding the karma of meditative concentration; it is not that [the Master] was unaware of this. Later students, being unable to reach such a level, instead resort to slanderous speech—this is truly lamentable.
It is like the fish-trap and the rabbit-snare: once the fish and the rabbit have been caught, the trap and snare may be forgotten.
This can be seen from the following passage.
To differentiate names and characteristics without knowing when to cease is like entering the ocean to count its sands—merely exhausting oneself in vain.
How could there be any fault in the study of the sūtras and śāstras? They were spoken from the golden mouth of our Buddha, the Tathāgata;
even their names cannot be heard in immeasurable lands, let alone seen. Thus, one knows that the teaching is not...
Those who are deluded cause themselves to be deluded by the teachings. An ancient worthy said: "One must possess the eye for reading scriptures when examining them;
if the eye is not clear, one will instead be dazzled by names and forms. To fail to investigate the mind-ground while being solely preoccupied with extensive learning—this is why it is said:"
Even if one studies extensively, it still results in greed. Who can turn back and know how to feel self-reproach? Wandering aimlessly, one becomes a guest in a foreign land;
failing to shoulder the essential style of our own school, one is like someone entering the sea to count its sands—merely exhausting oneself in vain.
Yet one is harshly rebuked by the Tathāgata: "What benefit is there in counting another's treasures?
The Tathāgata rebukes those of much learning; though they possess great erudition, they fail to attain realization. As the Sūtra says: "It is like a person counting another's treasures;
he himself has not even half a coin. Since it is not one's own treasure, even if one counts it until the end of the day, [it remains of no use].
Knowing the measure and quantity [of the Dharma], one must not indulge in its use; what benefit would that bring to oneself? Thus it is said:

"It is like spending one's entire life discoursing on medicine while remaining afflicted by a chronic illness. It is as if one were to inquire about the distance for a long journey yet fail to move a single step.
Those who catch the fish and forget the trap are rarely encountered among men; those who grasp the finger and mistake it for the moon are indeed numerous.
This is precisely its meaning.
"From of old I have stumbled, realizing my journey was in vain; for many years I have needlessly been a traveler in the winds and dust.
"From of old" means from beginningless time. "Stumbled" (cèngdèng) describes the manner of one whose progress does not advance. "In vain" (xū) refers to traveling without purpose.
This refers to traveling in vain without having reached one's destination.

From beginningless time until this very day, one has traversed the perilous paths of birth and death, needlessly exhausting oneself, yet never having truly trodden upon the road to Nirvana; hence it is said that one is "awakened to traveling in vain.
For many years one has pointlessly been a traveler in the dust and wind, like a worldly person drifting aimlessly between north and south.
A thousand li from home, one’s native land grows ever more distant; in vain does one become a traveler amidst the dust and wind. An ancient worthy said:
"Before one's gate there are endless paths; who is the person who has reached home?"
This refers to those of a perverted disposition who possess erroneous understanding and fail to comprehend the Tathāgata’s Perfect and Sudden teachings.
They claim that those who do not take refuge in the Triple Gem are like the ninety-six types of non-Buddhist heretics in India who rely on false teachers and give rise to various heterodox views;
thus, they are said to have "erroneous understanding. They fail to penetrate the Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s Mind-Ground.
Thus we know that undergoing immeasurable birth and death throughout immeasurable kalpas is entirely due to the teachings of false masters.

Because one did not encounter the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna as expounded by the Bodhisattvas, the Treatise says: "It would be better to undergo the sufferings of hell than to receive the names of the Buddhas;
it is not better to enjoy immeasurable pleasure while failing to hear the names of the Buddhas. This is because in the past...
For immeasurable kalpas, they undergo suffering and transmigrate through birth and death because they have not heard the name of the Buddha.
That they have not heard the name of the Buddha is entirely because they have encountered false teachers.
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles possess diligence but lack the Bodhicitta; the heretics possess cleverness but lack true wisdom.
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles diligently cultivate their practice to sever the views and afflictions of the triple world, returning seven times among humans and devas.
The dharma-gates they traverse and cultivate are indeed diligent, yet they drink the wine of quiescent extinction and lie upon the bed of Nirvana, failing to arise.
To cultivate the practice of benefiting others with a heart of great compassion, to receive sentient beings and bring them profit—this is the mind of the Way.

As for those who are clever but lack wisdom among the non-Buddhists: there were extremely brilliant scholars among the non-Buddhists of India who could recite the four Vedas, yet they did not understand the Buddha-nature.
Thus, Hanshan said: "In the world there are many people of great understanding, yet they study in ignorance."
They employ mere literary skill and do not worry about the fruits of the future; they know only how to create the causes of evil. Seeing the Buddha, they do not understand how to pay him homage;

seeing the Sangha, they instead give rise to redoubled anger. These are the types who commit the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, with the three poisons as their companions. When they die and enter hell, there will be no time when they emerge.
Throughout ancient and modern times, those of brilliant intellect have been driven by worldly wisdom and thus do not believe in Prajñā.
Indeed there is. An ancient worthy said: "Li Bai and Li Si were peerless in literature; yet these two men did not encounter the Record of the Empty King.
For how long have they vainly borne their clever minds? In the end, they could not penetrate through birth and death. The former sages bestowed such compassion;
how could it be that [the Buddhas] do not know [of our condition]?
They are both deluded and childish. They produce a conception of reality regarding an empty fist held up as a finger.

One who lacks wisdom is called "deluded" (*mūḍha*); a small child who lacks wisdom is called "childish" (*bāla*). Regarding the phrase "producing a conception of reality regarding an empty fist held up as a finger":
fools and children falsely imagine that which is empty to be truly existent, just as one might take yellow leaves to be [gold].
People take these as being real and true. The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has expounded a great treasury of the teachings;

all of it was produced by his heart of great compassion, emitting light according to conditions through his wondrous wisdom of non-action. He spoke of the existence of phenomena, or of the emptiness of phenomena;
he spoke of the sudden and the gradual, or of the partial and the perfect; he spoke of the indeterminate. Through various names and characteristics, he followed conditions and...
Each attains understanding accordingly. Those of inferior capacities give rise to attachments based on the literal words and fail to see the Buddha-nature;
it is like taking an empty fist and giving rise to the notion that it contains something real. The following text provides further analogies to clarify this point.
To mistake the finger for the moon is to exert effort in vain; within the phenomena of the sense organs and their objects, one falsely fabricates strange delusions.
If one is confused by taking the finger to be the moon, one is not only confused about the moon, but also confused about the finger itself, because one has identified the finger as the moon.
As the Sūtra says: "The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon. If one sees the moon, one understands what was pointed out."
Ultimately, it is not the moon. Therefore, those who study the Way are also like this.
If one takes the teaching to be the Buddha-nature, one is not only deluded regarding the Buddha-nature, but is also deluded regarding the teaching.

Because one takes the teaching to be the Buddha-nature, one is thereby misapplying one's meritorious practice. Thus we know that for those of middling or inferior faculties, if there were no Mahāyāna Prajñā...

Regarding the spiritual lineage (gotra), they are unable to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The locus of their ailment lies within the eighteen dharmas of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses;
therefore, it is said that they falsely fabricate monstrosities amidst the dharmas of the sense organs and objects.
"When not seeing a single dharma, one is the Tathāgata; only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara.
This single line is Yongjia’s best effort to drag one to the very threshold of the door; it merely lacks the lifting of the foot to step inside.

In the past, there was a man of long-standing virtue who, while studying the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, reached the passage: "All dharmas, from their very origin, are eternally in the aspect of quiescent extinction.
He rejoiced in this and constantly applied his mind to investigate its essence. He investigated it whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;

whether speaking, remaining silent, acting, performing tasks, lifting a spoon, or setting down chopsticks—there was no movement or activity he did not scrutinize. Yet, he attained nothing at all. This continued until the middle of spring.
In the second month of spring, one day while leaning against the railing and sitting idly, he heard the song of a yellow oriole in the tree and attained sudden enlightenment.
Realizing his former karmic conditions, he continued his previous verse: "All phenomena, from the very beginning, are eternally in the state of quiescent extinction;

when the spring is warm and the hundred flowers are red, the yellow oriole sings atop the willows. By observing the words of the venerable masters of the past and present through this, he came to understand them thoroughly.
The purpose of this is to seek the seal of approval from a teacher; once one is free from all obstructions in whatever is applied, one is truly entitled to be called Avalokiteśvara.
When one realizes this, karmic obstacles are originally empty; if one has not yet realized it, one must still repay past debts.
When one thoroughly understands that the nature of both sin and merit is empty, there is no longer any hindrance.

If a person resolves their mind to return to the source, the worlds of the ten directions all vanish away—how much more so the marks of sin and merit? Therefore, Master Sengzhao said: "The body of the five aggregates..."
It does not exist. The four great elements are originally empty. To bring one’s head to the edge of a white blade is just like cutting the spring breeze;
this is because karmic obstructions are originally empty. If one does not realize this and clings to the dharmas without letting go, then the law of cause and effect is like a form and its shadow.
Even if one has committed deeds throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they will not be forgotten; when causes and conditions meet, the retribution will surely return.
Because one receives [the consequences] oneself, it is said: "If one has not yet settled them, one must still repay past debts.
When hungry, one cannot eat even a king's banquet; when ill, how can one hope for recovery upon meeting a master physician?
For forty-nine years, he opened the gate of expedient means and revealed the true aspect.
Through various Dharma gates taught by the power of his great compassionate vows, he sought to guide and lead sentient beings; yet these beings themselves were unable to awaken and enter [the truth].

It is like a person in the world suffering from hunger who encounters the meal of a sovereign, where food fills a space ten feet square and all varieties of land and water creatures are fully prepared. Various...
It was delicious; yet upon seeing it, he immediately felt fear and did not dare to eat it.
It is like a person who has suffered from a chronic illness for a long time, who suddenly sees the physician Lu, the King of Physicians, Bianque;
he will surely give rise to doubt and hesitation and be unable to take the wondrous medicine, thereby knowing that his illness cannot be cured.
Practicing dhyāna while remaining within the realm of desire through the power of wisdom and insight—like a lotus born from fire, it can never be destroyed.
Those who practice the purity of dhyāna-nā while in the desire realm do so because they possess the power of prajñā-wisdom and insight.
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "In the realm of desire there is no dhyāna; why, Venerable Sir, do you say that there is meditative concentration?
The ancient worthy replied, "Ācārya, you only know that in the realm of desire there is no dhyāna; you do not realize that within the realm of dhyāna there is no desire.
You should know that the three realms all arise from what belongs to the one mind. As a sutra says: 'By extinguishing the three poisons, one exits the three realms and breaks the net of Māra. Now...
Regarding the phrase "the power of knowledge and vision": once the mind clearly perceives the Buddha-nature, then every place becomes a Buddha-work.
Why, then, speak of it reaching only as far as the Desire Realm? Therefore, it is called the "power of knowledge and vision."
Vīradatta committed a grave offense yet realized non-arising; he attained Buddhahood long ago and remains even now.
In the distant past, there was a bhikṣu named Vīradatta who suddenly failed in the prohibitions of the Tathāgata’s precepts.
Having committed the four root transgressions, he desired to purify himself and thus hung his three robes...
Standing upon the roof, he cried out in a loud voice, "I have committed a grave offense; who will perform repentance for me?
He continued to cry out in this manner until he reached a vihāra, where he encountered a venerable elder named Viśuddhara. [The elder] said, "Examine the nature of the offense;
it is ultimately unattainable. Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu Vīradatta attained sudden and great enlightenment, became endowed with the ten titles, and immediately departed for the eastern direction.
He attained equal and perfect enlightenment in this world and was named the Tathāgata Ratnacandra. He remains even until now;
therefore it is said that he attained Buddhahood long ago and still exists today.
With the lion’s roar, he speaks without fear, deeply lamenting those who are ignorant, stubborn, and callous.
The Buddhas preach the Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna with mastery and fearlessness, just as a lion roars with fearless sovereignty;
hence it is called "fearless preaching. "Deeply sighing" (*shen jia*) is an expression of profound lamentation.
"Dull-witted" (*meng chong*) means lacking intelligence. "Stubborn hide and sinew" (*wan pi zha*) refers to the extremely coarse and thick hide on the neck of an ox. This...
This is a metaphor for those of dull faculties in the Lesser Vehicle who, upon hearing the Great Dharma, are unable to awaken; thus they utter words of lamentation and grief.
They know only that committing grave offenses obstructs Bodhi, yet they do not see the Tathāgata’s revelation of the secret key.
They know only that committing the first four kinds of grave offenses obstructs the wondrous mind of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, yet they are unable to realize that the nature of these offenses is empty.
Thus, those who cannot escape from the realm of birth and death do so because they take lust and killing as their foundation, sinking into it without end.
If one possesses the lineage of the Mahāyāna, even when encountering such external objects, [one remains unshaken].
By generating the bodhicitta and returning from delusion to the truth, one is able to enter the Way.
This is like when Sudhana visited the woman Vasumitrā, who said to him: "I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'The Limit Beyond Greed.
I manifest my body in accordance with worldly pleasures. If there are sentient beings who see me for even a moment, speak with me for even a moment, or..."
If one grasps my hand, one will be freed from greed and desire and attain the samādhi of traveling everywhere to all Buddha-fields.

Furthermore, it is like when Sudhana visited King Anala; there were immeasurable fierce executioners brandishing weapons, and immeasurable sentient beings who had each committed offenses—some having their heads severed and some having their hands cut off. Having seen this, Sudhana made this [vow].
He asked, "How can you seek the Dharma in such a place? The King told Sudhana, "I have attained the Bodhisattva’s Illusion-like Samādhi.

One with a mind like mine would rather undergo the sufferings of the Avīci hell in the future than, for even a single thought-moment, inflict suffering upon a single mosquito or an ant, let alone a human being. Therefore, know that if there is one who possesses [the seed...]"

As for their nature: when they encounter external objects before them, they are immediately able to return to the source. Now, these followers of the Two Vehicles and those of lesser capacity are mired in the ritual matters of observing and violating precepts;
they focus exclusively on phenomenal dharmas and thus fail to see that the nature of both sin and merit is empty.

To clearly perceive the Buddha-nature is precisely what the Tathāgata did not reveal as a secret instruction. Therefore, the following text specifically cites [the cases of] sexual misconduct and killing.
These signs clarify past events.
There were two bhikṣus who committed sexual misconduct and murder; Pūrṇa and Śuddhipanthaka increased their karmic fetters through these acts.
Those who commit sexual misconduct and murder all incur fundamental grave offenses. As for "fireflies," in the Hīnayāna, they are like the light of a firefly.
It cannot dispel the darkness. In the past, there were two bhikṣus who built huts in the mountains to practice.
They maintained the pure precepts with firm resolve, without any transgression. One day, one bhikṣu went out, while the other remained in the hut in meditative concentration.
Suddenly, he fell asleep while sitting; thus, he became drowsy and was violated by a woodcutter’s daughter who had stolen his purity.
Consequently, his heart was displeased. Upon returning to the monk in the same hermitage, he recounted the matter in detail. That monk, filled with anger, immediately seized and pursued her.
Terrified, the woodcutter’s daughter fell into a deep pit and died. The bhikṣu’s affliction increased all the more, thinking, "One person has unintentionally committed an act of lust."
One person committed the offense of killing unintentionally; these two bhikṣus had both committed offenses without intent.
Together they went to the place of the Venerable Upāli to seek confession. The Venerable, according to the Hīnayāna, adjudged them guilty of an offense.
At that time, the two bhikṣus were uncertain and could not resolve their doubts; their confusion grew further, so they immediately went to the layman Vimalakīrti to confess.
He related the aforementioned matter. Vimalakīrti said, "It was improper for you to preach the Dharma without skillfully observing the capacities of the listeners.
These two bhikṣus have long cultivated the Mahāyāna; how could you compare the great ocean to the hoofprint of an ox?
Upāli’s Hīnayāna is like a firefly—its light cannot dispel the darkness. Therefore it is said: 'Upāli’s firefly-light increases the bonds of transgression.'"
The Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispelled all doubts, just as the brilliant sun melts away frost and snow.

While the Venerable Upāli exclusively employed the ritual methods of the Hīnayāna for repentance, asserting that certain offenses cannot be repented of, Vimalakīrti now expounded the Dharma-gate of the emptiness and signlessness of intrinsic nature through principle;
he thoroughly investigated the nature of offenses and found them ultimately non-existent.
It is attained. It is not within, not without, nor in between the two. It does not go to the past, it does not come from the future, and it does not abide in the present.

When sought throughout the three periods of time, it is utterly unattainable. At that moment, the two bhikṣus suddenly and instantaneously awakened to the fact that the nature of sin is empty and quiescent;
their minds became resolute, and they dwelt in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). As the Sūtra says: "If..."
One who wishes to repent should sit upright and contemplate the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). All transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can eliminate them.
Thus it is said: "It is just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow."
Inconceivable is the power of liberation; its wondrous function is as infinite as the sands of the Ganges.
"Inconceivable" means it cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed by the mouth. When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail;
when the mind wishes to think, deliberation vanishes. As the Sūtra says: "Even if the world were filled with beings like Śāriputra..."
One may contemplate and deliberate together, yet one cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. Upon reaching this point, there must be a mind of awakening;

only then will one clearly understand the liberation of the One Vehicle, the perfect and sudden Dharma-gate. Once this Dharma is realized, its wondrous function is as inexhaustible as the sands of the Ganges.
Therefore, it is said: "The wondrous function is like the sands of the Ganges; it is infinite."
"I venture to decline the toil of the fourfold offerings; even ten thousand taels of gold would be consumed [in vain].
One who has realized the Dharma is worthy of receiving the vast offerings of devas and humans.

Regarding those who have left the household life, if their bodies have departed from home but their minds remain unstained by the Path, they lack all that is taught in the various sūtras and śāstras regarding the requirements for being a *dakṣiṇīya* (one worthy of offerings). An ancient master said:
It is precisely what is meant when it is said that if one does not cultivate morality, clothing and food will be wasted.
As for the "four requisites," they are: first, clothing; second, bedding; third, food and drink; and fourth, medicine.
Regarding these four matters, within all the teachings, one must give rise to a sense of shame and remorse before using them. How could this practitioner alone fail to do so?
It is simply a matter of fact. Even ten thousand ounces of gold could purchase it;
yet grinding one's bones to powder would not suffice as recompense. A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends billions of worlds.
Regarding "grinding one's bones": it was as when the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita studied the *Prajñāpāramitā* in the City of Fragrance (*Gandhavatī*).
Having already attained the Dharma, he lamented that he had nothing to offer the World-Honored One. Suddenly, he encountered a wealthy and noble elder of the city who was unwell.
Desiring to obtain human marrow for his medicinal compound, he immediately struck his own bone to extract the marrow and sold it to the elder.
With the funds obtained, he purchased various flowers and incense to make offerings to the Buddha; from this, one can know the sincerity of his resolve.
As for "shattering the body," it refers to how Śākyamuni, during his causal stage, sacrificed his entire body to seek half a verse. I reflect upon these past events...
He departed to become a brahmin and practiced the bodhisattva path amidst the Snow Mountains.
At that time, no Buddha had appeared in the world, nor were there any sutras or teachings. Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested a terrifying form to personally test him.

Appearing before him in the guise of a rākṣasa, he recited half a verse: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. When the Bodhisattva heard this, [he...]
The verse-gatha brought joy to his heart, and he immediately rose from his seat. Looking around in the four directions, he saw nothing but silence;
he beheld only the rākṣasa, whom he asked: "Noble One, from where did you obtain this half-verse?
This half-verse is the dharma for realizing the Way of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. The rākṣasa replied: "It has already been seven days since I last ate."
The Rākṣasa spoke falsely. Then the Bodhisattva spoke again: "Noble One, if you would complete this verse for me, I shall be your disciple for the rest of my life.
The Rākṣasa replied, "Driven by hunger, I truly cannot speak.
The Bodhisattva spoke again: "Noble One, what do you eat? What I eat is only warm flesh; as for what I drink..."
[The Rākṣasa] would drink nothing but fresh blood. The Bodhisattva spoke again: "Noble One, if you can recite this sublime verse for me, I shall sacrifice my body as an offering to you.
At that time, the Rākṣasa immediately spoke the verse: "When birth and death have ceased, and cessation has also ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss.
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva immediately inscribed this verse upon a stone wall by the Bodhi tree.
Having finished speaking, he immediately climbed a tall tree and threw himself down.
Before he had even reached the ground, the rākṣasa resumed the form of Śakra and caught him in mid-air, setting him down on level ground. Filled with shame and remorse, he offered praise;

by virtue of these causes and conditions, he transcended twelve kalpas and will attain the unsurpassed path before Maitreya. Thus it is said: "A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion [kalpas]."
The King of Dharmas, most supreme and victorious, realized by all Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Among kings, he is the Dharma-King; his station transcends that of a hundred kings, hence he is called the "King of Dharmas.
Transcending the three realms and walking alone upon the Great Way, he is thus called "most supreme and victorious. This extends even to the past, future, and present.
Innumerable Buddhas have all realized this; all the venerable elders of the world have all realized this.
The infinite clusters of dharmas and all gateways of meaning do not transcend this. As the Sūtra says: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can know it."
"Only the Buddha" refers specifically to Śākyamuni, the Lord of Transformation. "Together with the Buddhas" refers to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Thus it is said "only," meaning not one Buddha, nor two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but rather that the Buddhas of the ten directions all together realize this Dharma;
hence it is said, "the Tathāgatas of the ten directions collectively testify to it."
I now explain this wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). Those who believe and accept it will all be in accord with it.
Only this mental dharma is like the worldly wish-fulfilling gem; it possesses all functional powers without end.
The Fourth Patriarch said to Chan Master Niu-tou Rong: "A hundred thousand wondrous gates all return to the single square inch [of the mind]. The River...

All meritorious virtues reside within the source of the mind. All gates of samādhi, all gates of wisdom, and all gates of practice are fully endowed with the wondrous functions of supernatural powers;
these are all within your own mind. Afflictions and karmic obstructions are originally empty and quiescent.
All retributions are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to escape, and there is no bodhi to seek.
The nature of humans and non-humans is equal. The Great Way is vast and empty, transcending thought and deliberation.
You have now attained such a Dharma; it lacks nothing and is no different from that of the Buddha. There is no other dharma. Simply allow the mind to be at ease;
do not engage in contemplative practices, nor do you need to fixate the mind. Do not give rise to greed, and take care not to harbor sorrow or anxiety.

Vast and unimpeded, one moves freely in all directions. Neither performing good nor committing evil, walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, whatever meets the eye or encounters the conditions is entirely the wondrous function of the Buddha. Therefore, it is said that those who believe and accept this are all in accord with it.
One sees clearly that there is not a single thing, nor is there a person, nor is there a Buddha.
Within the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are no provisional names of "sentient beings" or "Buddhas. Within the state of equality, there are no forms of "self" or "other.
Thus, there is neither thing, nor person, nor Buddha. Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Subhūti, empty space is empty and pure."
Because of purity, form is pure; because form is pure, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) is pure. Why is this?
Whether it be the emptiness of emptiness being pure, form being pure, or all-knowledge being pure, they are non-dual and not divided;
they are without distinction and without interruption. Therefore, it is said: "One sees clearly that there is not a single thing; there is neither person nor Buddha."
The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the ocean; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.
The three thousandfold world-system within the nature of awakening is like a single bubble upon the water.
Not only is the great trichiliocosm a bubble upon the water, but the entirety of the worlds throughout the ten directions exists within the nature of awakening.
The interim state is like a single bubble upon the water. As stated in the realization of perfect penetration attained by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:
"From delusive ignorance comes empty space; based on space, the world is established. When thought settles, it forms the land; through cognition and vision, there arise sentient beings."
"Emptiness arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean; therefore it is said that the sands and realms of the great trichiliocosm are but bubbles in the sea.
"All sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning" means they are like the spark from a flint—suddenly appearing and leaving no trace, so difficult to grasp.
Thus the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Because internal emptiness is pure, the realm of form, the realm of the eye, and the realm of visual consciousness..."
The sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition are pure; the forms of the form realm, up to and including the sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition, are pure.
Therefore, the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) is pure. Thus it is said that all noble ones are like a flash of lightning.
"Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one's head, the perfection of concentration and wisdom would never be lost.
Regarding "even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one's head," the tradition says:

By the power of the practice of a Bodhisattva dwelling in the twenty-eighth stage, there was a Mara King who said to the Bodhisattva, "You must step down from this position. If you do not step down, I shall..."
A flying wheel of glowing-hot iron will spin upon the crown of your head, shattering your physical form into mere atoms.
At that time, by virtue of the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattva’s perfected clarity of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā-suvibhakta*), he shall not lose his station;

meanwhile, the hosts of Māras will instead retreat and fall away. Because the Bodhisattva’s concentration and wisdom increase ever more brightly, it is said: "The perfection of concentration and wisdom is ultimately..."
It is not lost. The sun might become cold; the moon might become hot. Yet no demons can destroy the True Teaching.
Since the nature of the sun is inherently hot, how could it be said to be cold? Since the nature of the moon is inherently cold, how could it be said to be hot? Thus we know that the [demons]...
Māra cannot destroy its true exposition. When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, Māra’s palace trembles and his evil followers take refuge;
how then could he ever subvert the holy word? As for the claim that the sun could be made cold and the moon made hot—

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "The moon might be made hot, and the sun might be made cold, but the Four Noble Truths taught by the Buddha cannot be made otherwise.
Now, Yongjia employs this to clarify that the various māras cannot destroy the true teaching of Prajñā.
An elephant carriage, towering and majestic, advances in vain upon its path; who has ever seen a mantis able to block its tracks?
The Mahāyāna Dharma-gate propagated by the Bodhisattva cannot be obstructed by any demons.
It is like an elephant carriage advancing with imposing grandeur—how could a tiny insect like a mantis possibly block its wheels? Thus it was in the past...
Duke Zhuang of Qi was out hunting when a mantis raised its legs, intending to strike his chariot wheel. He asked his charioteer, "What kind of insect is this?
The charioteer replied, "This is a mantis. Duke Zhuang said, "With such minute strength, it seeks to resist a great chariot;
it does not measure its own power. Now, Yongjia has briefly entered the conditions of the world...
He realized the supramundane noble Dharma and made it easy to understand. Now, the Dharma flows throughout the realm of Jambudvīpa and its teachings fill the Dragon Palaces;
how could the various lesser sages and hosts of māras possibly create obstructions or hindrances? Thus it is said: "Who has ever seen a cicada able to block the tracks of a chariot?"
A great elephant does not travel upon the narrow paths of a rabbit; one of great awakening is not constrained by minor details.
The realms traversed by Bodhisattvas of the Mahāyāna possess such extraordinary merit that they are beyond the knowledge of humans and devas.
As for the dharmaparyāyas encountered by those of the Two Vehicles, their qualities differ in degree. To make this easily understood, the worldly analogy of the elephant and the rabbit is employed.
For example, the path traversed by a great elephant can only be accommodated by a broad highway; it cannot be reached via the narrow trails of small rabbits.
Thus it is said, "The great elephant does not travel upon rabbit paths. Those who have attained great enlightenment are not constrained by minor details.
One who has realized their nature cannot be scrutinized through phenomenal appearances, nor can they be bound by the observance or violation of the precepts and Vinaya. Their actions—
This is difficult to fathom. For example, there was the novice Gao who did not receive the precepts, and Yaoshan who did not study the sutras;
thus it is said that "great awakening is not constrained by minor details."
Do not slander the vast expanse with your narrow, biased views. Since you have not yet realized it, I shall now resolve this for you:

Unsurpassed Prajñā is accessible only to those of the highest faculties and the most superior capacities; those of middling or inferior disposition find it ultimately difficult to grasp or model after.
For this reason, the three realms are vast and the six paths are desolate; all are merely empty lives and vain deaths. As the Sūtra says: "It is, for example,"
A hundred thousand mosquitoes and gadflies are gathered in a single vessel, chirping and clamoring together with distended bellies in wild agitation;
they do not know the vast expanse of the great void. This illustrates that those of small capacity cannot give rise to the bodhicitta or enter the realm of the Mahāyāna.
Now Yongjia fears that people of the world may lack sufficient faith and thus give rise to groundless slander. It is as if...
It is like a fool grasping a tube to peer at the sky; because his own vision is narrow and limited, he slanders the boundless azure expanse.

Whose fault is this? Regarding that single phrase which I have now resolved for you—one that the entire Great Canon (*Tripitaka*) cannot fully elucidate, yet for which the six generations of Patriarchs have praise to offer—it is known that from the time of our predecessors...
The Sage opened the gate of expedient means to guide those who follow behind. He granted a single thread of the Way, briefly revealing his style and character.
Let not this final word be misquoted.

During the Yuanfeng era, I went with two or three friends from the National University to Donglin at Xiangguo Temple.

There, we met with several officials of the Han Garden, including Lord Deng Zifa, the Zilongtu, Haoran, and Mingfu; it was there that I first encountered the Master amidst their company as they engaged in leisurely discourse on the Way.
I knew what was harbored within the Master’s mind. Subsequently, hearing that the Master had been granted robes in the inner palace, I went to offer my congratulations and saw him once more.
He spoke with words like pearls and gems, revealing his true vision; he was elegant and possessed the refined character of the ancients. I especially regretted having met him so late.
Students of the world often suffer from holding divergent views and being biased toward a single corner, failing to realize the Great Way.
Those who ultimately engage in mutual disparagement are all like this. The Master’s nature was humble and harmonious.

Beyond his dedication to the transmission of the Dharma and the joy of Chan meditation, he was well-versed in the sources of the teachings and delighted in literature; that he did not allow these different paths to divide his resolve is truly commendable.

In the second month of spring in the first year of the Yuanyou era, while passing by Sishang, I met the Venerable Yuanming, who had come from Mount Kuanglu and received what the Master had bestowed upon him.

I chanted and contemplated it with a sense of refreshing clarity; thus I knew that what our Master maintained was lofty and simple, unmixed with profit or fame, as he wandered at ease beyond the fray of competition.
In the *bingzi* year of the Shaosheng era, I resigned my office and traveled alone on horseback to the Ministry of Personnel for my official evaluation.
Upon reaching Shouchun, I met my friend Wu Chunfu, who presented to me the Master’s commentary on the *Yongjia Zhengdao Ge*, which brilliantly illuminates the Tathāgata.
A great ocean of wisdom, benefiting the fourfold assembly—how could this be due to minor causes? The Master was a native of Zhejiang and was a dharma heir of Chan Master Yuanzhao.
Delighted by his former acquaintance, I have respectfully inscribed this at the end of the scroll. Recorded on the full moon of the first month of summer in this year by Tian Ni.
Every day, Master Shishi of Yongjia ascended the seat to uphold the orthodox command. He distilled the essential points of the Dharma to demonstrate the realization of the Way.
Remaining silent for a moment, he gave a single strike with his whisk and asked, "Do you understand? Thereupon, he spoke a gāthā.

A single blow empties heaven and earth, Startling the dead from their blindness and deafness. The numinous light spans from antiquity to the present, Pervading throughout the entire Dharma-realm. *Phonetic Glossary:* Jīng (驚): To startle Kāi (開): To open Sǐ (死): Dead Máng (盲): Blind Lóng (聾): Deaf Líng (靈): Numinous Guāng (光): Light Jìn (今): Present Gǔ (古): Antiquity Biàn (徧): Pervasive Hán (含): Containing Fǎjiè (法界): Dharma-realm Zhōng (中): Within Yīnshì (音釋): Phonetic glossary *Note: This is a poetic verse likely from a Chan or Zen Buddhist text, expressing the sudden awakening that shatters ignorance and reveals the eternal, all-pervading nature of reality.*

jiāo (顦) is also written as jiāo (憔). Lìn (恡): Pronounced lìn (音吝), with the initial sound of lì (力) and the final rhyme of rèn (刃); it means stinginess.

[The character] *yǔ* and *hài*, with the second tone (*qiè*). It means the galloping of a horse; it also means to be ignorant.

Huò (pronounced like "huo"). Xiè (the radical is *ju* with the tone *ài*):
